facts.t: The **NYHA classification** grades limitation by symptoms: class I has no limitation, class **II** has slight limitation with symptoms on **ordinary activity**, class **III** has marked limitation with symptoms on **less-than-ordinary activity**, and class IV has symptoms at rest; classes II and III are comfortable at rest.

**Aortic regurgitation** gives a large-volume, bounding, collapsing (**water-hammer**) pulse from a large stroke volume and low diastolic pressure, but a **bounding pulse is not specific** to AR: it also occurs in other high-output states such as anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, patent ductus arteriosus and fever.

**Pulsus parvus et tardus** is a small-volume, slow-rising pulse, best appreciated by careful palpation of the **carotid arteries**, and is the pulse of **severe aortic stenosis** from fixed outflow obstruction; a **bisferiens** pulse instead suggests mixed aortic stenosis and regurgitation.
**Pulsus alternans** is beat-to-beat variability in pulse amplitude (alternating strong and weak beats) and signals **severe left ventricular impairment**.

**Pulsus paradoxus** is an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure of **more than 10 mmHg during inspiration** (a fall of up to 10 mmHg is physiological) and is the classic sign of **cardiac tamponade**; it does not characterise severe aortic regurgitation.

**Korotkoff sounds** mark systolic and diastolic pressure and have **5 phases**: phase 4 is **muffling** and phase 5 is **disappearance**; diastolic pressure is recorded at **phase 5**, except in aortic regurgitation and in children, where both muffling and disappearance are recorded.
Blood pressure readings are falsely raised by an **unsupported arm** and by a **full urinary bladder**, while an **auscultatory gap** causes **underestimation** of the systolic pressure.

The normal **jugular venous pulse** has three positive waves, **'a', 'c' and 'v'**; the **'a' wave** follows the **P wave** of the ECG (atrial contraction) and the venous pulse **collapses during systole** (x descent). The centre of the **right atrium** lies about **5 cm below the sternal angle** (angle of Louis), the reference point for measuring jugular venous pressure.

The **JVP falls during inspiration** in normal individuals; a paradoxical **rise on inspiration (Kussmaul sign)** is seen in **constrictive pericarditis** and is absent in tamponade. A **raised JVP** occurs in right ventricular failure, tricuspid stenosis, tricuspid regurgitation and superior vena cava obstruction.

A **prominent 'a' wave** occurs when the right atrium contracts against resistance: **tricuspid stenosis**, **pulmonary stenosis**, pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy. The 'a' wave is **absent in atrial fibrillation** (no atrial contraction), and **cannon 'a' waves** occur in **complete heart block** when the atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve.

**Tricuspid regurgitation** gives a raised JVP with a prominent **'v' wave** and **systolic expansion** of the neck veins (with a pulsatile liver), not a giant 'a' wave. Loss of the 'a' wave with **systolic expansion of the neck veins in the absence of significant tricuspid regurgitation** suggests **atrial fibrillation**.
**Mitral facies** (mild cyanosis of the lips, cheeks and malar prominences, sometimes called malar rash) is seen in **severe, long-standing mitral stenosis** without finger clubbing.

Peripheral stigmata of **infective endocarditis** include **Osler nodes** (painful, raised lesions on the hands and feet, an immunologic phenomenon), **splinter haemorrhages** under the nails and **clubbing**; Osler nodes are NOT a Jones criterion for rheumatic fever.

**Clubbing** is associated with **right-to-left shunting** (cyanotic congenital heart disease) and infective endocarditis; it is not common in heart failure, and a patent foramen ovale is not a common cause.

**Central cyanosis** is seen in warm as well as cold areas and is best observed in warm areas such as the **tongue and buccal mucosa**. **Absent dorsalis pedis pulsations** may be a normal anatomical variant, and **xanthelasma palpebrarum** may be seen in familial hypercholesterolaemia. Features of **Marfan syndrome** should prompt investigation for **aortic root dilatation or aneurysm**.

The **normal apex impulse** is localised within the midclavicular line and lasts **less than two-thirds of systole**; a **dilated right ventricle** causes a **diffuse apical impulse** and a left parasternal impulse, as in atrial septal defect.

The apex is **tapping (slapping)** and undisplaced in **mitral stenosis** (isolated MS does not enlarge the left ventricle), **hyperdynamic and displaced** downwards and outwards in **mitral regurgitation** and **aortic regurgitation** (volume overload; in severe AR the apex is in the 6th space at the anterior axillary line, localised and hyperkinetic), and **heaving (sustained)** in **aortic stenosis** and hypertension (pressure overload).
**Mitral stenosis** can cause a **palpable first heart sound**, and right ventricular enlargement gives a diffuse apex rather than a localised one.

The **first heart sound (S1)** is produced mainly by **mitral valve closure**; it is **accentuated (loud, snapping)** in mitral stenosis while the valve is pliable and becomes **muffled** when the valve is heavily calcified, and it is **soft/muffled in mitral regurgitation**.

The **aortic component of S2 (A2)** is **soft, weak or absent in severe aortic stenosis**, which gives a **single** second heart sound; **pulmonary stenosis** likewise makes the **pulmonary component (P2) soft and delayed**, not loud.

**Reversed (paradoxical) splitting** of S2 occurs with delayed left ventricular emptying in **severe aortic stenosis** (and left bundle branch block); **wide splitting** occurs in **complete right bundle branch block**, while **fixed splitting** is the pattern of atrial septal defect. Reversed splitting is not a sign of pulmonary hypertension.

The **third heart sound (S3)** is a **low-pitched** sound in **early diastole** produced by **rapid passive ventricular filling**; it may be **physiological in children and young adults** but in adults it indicates volume overload or heart failure (e.g. over the apex in mitral regurgitation and left heart failure).

The **fourth heart sound (S4)** is a **late diastolic (presystolic)** sound produced by **atrial systole** forcing blood into a **stiff ventricle**; it is **always abnormal**, is classically associated with **hypertension** and aortic stenosis with left ventricular hypertrophy, and is **lost in atrial fibrillation** because effective atrial contraction is absent.

The **opening snap** of mitral stenosis is an **early diastolic** sound heard over the apex and left parasternal border that denotes a **pliable, non-calcified valve** and disappears when the valve is heavily calcified; a **narrow (short) S2-opening snap interval**, with the snap close to S2, indicates **severe mitral stenosis** from high left atrial pressure.

An extra sound **shortly after S1** in a young woman with atypical chest pain and palpitation is a **non-ejection (mid-systolic) click** of **mitral valve prolapse**; the murmur of subvalvular aortic stenosis is an ejection murmur **without** an ejection click.

**Mitral stenosis** gives a loud S1, an opening snap and a **low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with presystolic accentuation** (in sinus rhythm; accentuation is lost in atrial fibrillation), with a **loud P2** when pulmonary hypertension develops.

**Mitral regurgitation** gives a muffled S1, an apical **S3**, and a soft blowing **pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla** (best in the left lateral position, not increased by inspiration); **posterior leaflet prolapse** directs the jet anteriorly so the murmur radiates to the **base but not to the carotids**.

**Aortic stenosis** gives a **late-peaking ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) systolic murmur** best heard over the **aortic area and radiating to the carotids**, with a soft A2 and a single or paradoxically split S2; late peaking reflects severity. The **Gallavardin phenomenon** is radiation of the high-frequency component of the AS murmur to the **apex**, where it may mimic mitral regurgitation.

**Aortic regurgitation** gives an **early diastolic decrescendo murmur** best heard over the **second aortic area and left sternal border**, often with a wide pulse pressure (e.g. 160/40) and peripheral signs such as **pistol-shot** sounds over the femoral artery.

The **Austin Flint murmur** is a **mid-diastolic apical murmur of functional mitral stenosis** that denotes **severe aortic regurgitation**: the regurgitant jet partially closes the **anterior mitral leaflet**. Unlike true mitral stenosis it has **no presystolic accentuation** and no loud S1 or opening snap.

**Right-sided murmurs increase with inspiration (Carvallo sign)**, while left-sided murmurs are louder on expiration: **tricuspid regurgitation** gives a **pansystolic murmur over the left parasternal area** increasing with inspiration, and **pulmonary stenosis** gives an **ejection systolic murmur** increasing with inspiration.

**Pulmonary hypertension** gives a **loud, palpable pulmonary component of S2 (P2)** with prominent pulsation in the **pulmonary area** (left 2nd intercostal space), a left parasternal heave and congested pulsating neck veins.

On **dynamic auscultation**, sustained isometric **handgrip** (increased afterload) **increases** the murmurs of **aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation and ventricular septal defect**, while the murmurs of **aortic stenosis** and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy decrease.

On the ECG at 25 mm/s, each **small square** on the horizontal axis represents **0.04 seconds**; with regular R-R intervals the heart rate is **300 divided by the R-R interval in large squares** (or 1500 divided by small squares).

The normal **P wave** is **positive in lead II** and **negative in aVR**, **less than 120 ms** in duration and **less than 2.5 mm** in amplitude, and may be **biphasic in V1**. **Right atrial enlargement** gives a tall peaked P wave of **more than 2.5 mm** (P pulmonale) with normal duration.
A **broad, notched P wave (P mitrale)** in lead II reflects **left atrial enlargement** and is a clue to **mitral stenosis**.

The **PR interval** is measured from the **beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex** (normal **120-200 ms**) and represents the time from **initial stimulation of the atria to initial stimulation of the ventricles**, including conduction through the AV junction.
The **QRS duration** is normally **less than 100 ms**, **100-120 ms** in incomplete bundle branch block and **more than 120 ms** in complete bundle branch block.
Chest lead **V2** is placed in the **fourth intercostal space just to the left of the sternum** (V1 is in the same space on the right).

**Left axis deviation** shows a predominantly positive QRS in **lead I** with a negative QRS in **aVF** (and lead III), while **right axis deviation** shows a negative QRS in lead I with positive inferior leads.

**Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)** shows high voltage with a **tall R in the left leads and a deep S in the right precordial leads**; **LVH with strain** adds **ST depression and T-wave inversion** in the lateral leads, as in systemic hypertension. Voltage criteria are only suggestive: **echocardiography confirms** hypertrophy.

**Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)** shows a **dominant R in V1 with right axis deviation** and occurs in **severe pulmonary stenosis**, **isolated tight mitral stenosis** and **primary pulmonary hypertension**, but not in isolated aortic stenosis (which gives LVH).
**Left bundle branch block (LBBB)** shows a **wide QRS with a broad, notched R in the lateral leads and a deep S in V1-V3**, with discordant ST-T changes.
**Right bundle branch block (RBBB)** shows a wide QRS with an **rSR' (M-shaped) pattern in V1** and a wide S wave in the lateral leads.
**Hyperkalaemia** gives **tall, peaked T waves with a widened QRS** on the ECG.
A **normal ECG** shows a normal axis, a narrow QRS complex and no ST-segment changes.

**Echocardiography** is the investigation of choice when cardiac disease is suspected from dyspnoea, a displaced apex, jugular venous distension and cardiomegaly, and it confirms ventricular hypertrophy suggested by ECG voltage criteria.

**Exercise ECG** is used to assess ECG changes with exercise in patients with **suspected coronary artery disease** (e.g. typical stable angina with a normal resting ECG); **beta-blockers should be withheld 24 hours before** the test because they blunt the heart-rate response.
Patients with chest pain may be evaluated with **exercise ECG, coronary angiography and thallium (myocardial perfusion) scanning**.
**Holter monitoring** (24-hour ECG) is used for **recurrent syncope** and **recurrent palpitations** when the resting ECG shows no abnormality.
**CT coronary angiography** uses iodinated contrast and is avoided in **chronic kidney disease**.
An **electrophysiology (EP) study** is indicated for assessment of **supraventricular tachycardia** and for **ablation of an accessory pathway**.

**Atrial fibrillation (AF)** shows an **irregularly irregular** rhythm with **no P waves** and a fibrillatory baseline; clinically it gives a markedly irregular pulse and loss of the jugular venous 'a' wave and of S4.

In **AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis**, treatment is **rate control** (beta-blocker, or digoxin) plus **warfarin anticoagulation for life** to prevent systemic embolism and stroke; direct oral anticoagulants are not used in rheumatic mitral stenosis. In AF with a fast rate and a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle, **rate or rhythm control is the first intervention**.

Any **haemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmia** (hypotension, pulmonary congestion, cold extremities, unresponsiveness) is treated with immediate **DC cardioversion**: unstable AF with a rapid response, unstable supraventricular tachycardia and unstable **ventricular tachycardia** alike.
Elderly patients with **aortic stenosis and atrial fibrillation** also receive **lifelong oral anticoagulation**, guided by stroke-risk score.
**Atrial flutter** shows regular **saw-tooth flutter waves**, often with **2:1 conduction** or a **variable block** giving an irregular ventricular response.
**Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)** is a very fast, **regular, narrow-complex** tachycardia with no visible sinus P waves.
**Sinus tachycardia** is a regular narrow-complex tachycardia of about 100-120/min with a **P wave before every QRS** and a normal PR interval, unlike SVT.
An **accelerated junctional rhythm** is a regular narrow-complex rhythm at about **60-100/min** with **no sinus P waves**.
**Ventricular tachycardia (VT)** is a regular **wide-complex** tachycardia: **monomorphic VT** has uniform wide QRS complexes, while **polymorphic VT** shows twisting complexes of changing amplitude.
A **premature ventricular contraction (PVC)** is an **early, wide, bizarre beat with no preceding P wave**.
**Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome** is ventricular **pre-excitation** through an **accessory pathway**, shown by a **short PR interval with a delta wave**.
**Sinus bradycardia** in an **asymptomatic athlete** (regular rhythm around 50/min with normal P-QRS complexes) is **physiological** and needs **no pacemaker**.
**First-degree heart block** is a **PR interval over 200 ms** with **every P wave conducted** to a QRS complex.
**Second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)** block shows **progressive PR prolongation** until an atrial impulse is blocked and produces no QRS complex.
**Second-degree Mobitz type II** block shows **intermittently non-conducted P waves with a constant PR interval**, not preceded by PR prolongation.

**Complete heart block** shows **AV dissociation** (independent P waves and a slow regular ventricular rate) and causes **syncope**; symptomatic bradyarrhythmia with conduction failure requires **pacemaker insertion**. Dropped beats with intact P waves indicate **impaired AV nodal conduction**, which may follow vagal stimuli such as micturition.
**Modifiable** risk factors for coronary artery disease include **smoking, obesity and hyperlipidaemia**; **age** is a non-modifiable risk factor.

**Stable (chronic) angina** is retrosternal chest tightness lasting a few minutes, **precipitated by exertion and relieved by rest**, with a stationary course and often a normal resting ECG; treatment is **aspirin, a statin, a beta-blocker and nitrates**, while loop diuretics and tirofiban (a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor) have no role in stable angina. With a normal resting ECG, **exercise ECG** is the next diagnostic step.

**Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)** comprises **STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina**; **variant (vasospastic) angina** is not part of ACS. **NSTEMI is distinguished from unstable angina by elevation of cardiac enzymes (troponin)**: unstable angina shows a crescendo pattern with dynamic ST depression but repeatedly **normal enzymes**, while NSTEMI shows ST depression with **raised troponin**. A normal troponin does **not** exclude typical angina, and typical pain may radiate to the jaw or present as isolated epigastric pain.

In a patient with severe chest pain who is vitally stable, the **first step is a 12-lead ECG** (within 10 minutes of arrival), before enzymes, echocardiography or angiography; equal pulses and blood pressure in both arms with an S4 favour ACS over dissection or pulmonary embolism.

In **NSTEMI**, **aspirin is the first step**, followed by a P2Y12 inhibitor; immediate primary PCI is not routine as it is in STEMI, but **invasive coronary angiography is indicated in high-risk** non-ST-elevation ACS.

**Anterior STEMI** shows ST elevation in the anterior leads: **V1-V3** indicates **anteroseptal** infarction, V1-V4/V5 an anterior infarction, and ST elevation across anterior and lateral leads an **extensive anterolateral** infarction, often with reciprocal ST depression inferiorly.
**Inferior STEMI** shows ST elevation in **leads II, III and aVF** with reciprocal changes; marked **ST depression in V1-V3** indicates posterior extension (**inferoposterior STEMI**).

In **STEMI**, **primary percutaneous coronary intervention (pPCI)** is the **gold standard** and is preferred over fibrinolysis when the anticipated time from diagnosis to PCI is **under 120 minutes** (transfer for pPCI even from a non-PCI hospital if it is close); if timely pPCI is impossible, **fibrinolytic therapy is given immediately** and the patient is transferred. A **loading dose of aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor** (clopidogrel or ticagrelor) is given during transfer, oxygen only if hypoxic, and **dual antiplatelet therapy is continued for up to 12 months**.
**Contraindications to thrombolytic therapy** for STEMI include **intracranial neoplasm, active internal bleeding and recent haemorrhagic stroke**.

**Ventricular free wall rupture** after myocardial infarction presents with sudden severe chest pain followed rapidly by **pulseless electrical activity**: an unrecordable pulse with sinus tachycardia on the monitor.

Complications of myocardial infarction include **ventricular tachycardia, heart failure and left ventricular aneurysm**; a **left ventricular aneurysm** itself predisposes to **ventricular tachycardia, heart failure and left ventricular thrombus**. An **old anterior MI** shows Q waves with persistent ST elevation in the anterior leads.
**Systemic hypertension** is diagnosed when blood pressure is **140/90 mmHg or higher**, and **essential uncomplicated hypertension is usually asymptomatic**.

**Secondary hypertension** should be suspected with **onset before age 25 or after age 60**, **resistant hypertension**, poor response to previously effective therapy, or **paroxysmal attacks** of hypertension with palpitation, pallor, sweating and tremors; severe hypertension in a young patient is more likely secondary (e.g. **renal artery stenosis, coarctation of the aorta** or intrinsic renal disease) than essential.
**Routine investigations** in hypertension include **ECG, fasting blood glucose, fasting lipids, and serum creatinine and urea**; urine protein electrophoresis is not routine.
The blood pressure **target is below 130/80 mmHg**, including in **diabetic nephropathy with macro-albuminuria**.
**Non-pharmacological therapy** for hypertension includes **exercise 30 minutes a day**, **more fruit and vegetables**, **weight reduction** and **stopping smoking**.

**ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the preferred starting drugs in diabetes**; in **pregnancy, methyldopa is safe** while **ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated**, as they are in **angioedema** and in **bilateral renal artery stenosis**.
Drugs used to treat hypertension include **beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors and centrally acting drugs**; alpha-adrenergic stimulants (agonists) are not antihypertensive therapy.

**Hypertensive emergency** presents with **acute target-organ damage** and needs immediate intravenous therapy, whereas **hypertensive urgency** has no target-organ damage and blood pressure is lowered **gradually over 24-48 hours with oral medication**.
In **resistant hypertension**, consider **non-compliance, drug interactions, excessive sodium intake, alcohol** and **renovascular disease**; liver cell failure is not a cause.

**Isolated left-sided heart failure** causes **orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea**, **bilateral fine basal crepitations** and an apical **S3 gallop**; the liver is not enlarged and pulsating, and right hypochondrial pain is not a feature.

**Isolated right-sided heart failure** causes **bilateral lower-limb oedema**, an **enlarged, pulsating liver** with **right hypochondrial pain and tenderness**, a **tricuspid-area S3** and a **pansystolic tricuspid murmur increasing with inspiration**; bilateral basal rales are a left-sided sign and are absent in isolated right failure.

Signs of heart failure include **congested pulsating neck veins**, an **S3 gallop**, **bilateral basal crepitations** and **bilateral pitting lower-limb oedema**; **central cyanosis is not** a sign of heart failure.
**Pulmonary oedema** presents with acute breathlessness and a cough producing **pink, frothy sputum**, with crackles and wheezes on auscultation.

Heart failure is classified by ejection fraction: **HFrEF (reduced) is EF 40% or below**, **mid-range (mildly reduced) is EF 41-49%**, and **HFpEF (preserved) is EF 50% or above**; HFpEF may show concentric hypertrophy with a preserved EF (e.g. 60%) in a hypertensive patient with LVH.

Treatment of **heart failure with reduced EF** includes **loop diuretics** for congestion, **ACE inhibitors**, **beta-blockers** (e.g. bisoprolol, started at a **low dose and titrated up**, never at the maximum dose in a decompensated patient) and **angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI)**, which improve prognosis; **digoxin** is used for rate control in AF. **Calcium channel blockers (calcium antagonists) are avoided** in HFrEF.

**Rheumatic heart disease** is the **commonest cause of mitral stenosis**; rheumatic mitral stenosis shows **fibrosis of the leaflets with fusion of the commissures**, and patients with post-rheumatic valve disease receive **secondary prophylaxis with long-acting penicillin**.

**Mitral stenosis** presents with progressive dyspnoea, nocturnal cough and **haemoptysis**, **palpitation from atrial fibrillation**, **systemic embolism** (e.g. stroke with hemiplegia) and **dysphagia** from a hugely enlarged left atrium; the chest X-ray shows a **near-normal left ventricular size with a prominent left atrial border**, and a large 'v' wave in the JVP indicates associated **tricuspid regurgitation**.

In **mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation**, the **presystolic accentuation disappears** (no atrial contraction) and the patient needs **lifelong warfarin anticoagulation, continued even after balloon mitral valvotomy**. **Tachycardia is poorly tolerated** in MS because it shortens diastolic filling time and **raises the trans-mitral pressure gradient**, which can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema.
Acute pulmonary oedema in mitral stenosis (e.g. from new-onset AF) or in aortic regurgitation is treated first with **intravenous diuretics**.

Complications of **long-standing isolated mitral stenosis** are **atrial fibrillation, systemic embolism, pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular dilatation and dysfunction**, with right-sided heart failure; **left ventricular dilatation is NOT** a complication of isolated MS.

**Balloon (percutaneous) mitral valvotomy** is preferred over valve replacement for a **pliable, non-calcified valve with minimal subvalvular disease**, signalled by an **opening snap**; it is **contraindicated** by **severe calcification** (high Wilkins score), **significant mitral regurgitation**, **left atrial thrombus** and associated severe aortic stenosis or regurgitation, while **mild mitral regurgitation** is not a contraindication.

**Mitral regurgitation** is caused by **rheumatic heart disease** (the leading cause in **developing countries**), **mitral valve prolapse / myxomatous degeneration**, **ischaemic** disease and **infective endocarditis**; any part of the mitral apparatus (leaflets, annulus, chordae, papillary muscles, left atrium or left ventricle) can be responsible, and **dilated cardiomyopathy** causes **functional** MR.

**Mitral regurgitation** gives a **hyperdynamic apex shifted outwards and downwards**, a **muffled S1**, an **apical S3**, and a **pansystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla**, louder in the left lateral position; reversed splitting of S2 is not a feature. The chest X-ray shows **left atrial enlargement** (bulge of the heart waist, elevated left main bronchus, double density, oesophagus pushed backwards), **left ventricular enlargement** and pulmonary congestion.

**Acute and chronic MR have different haemodynamics**: in **acute severe MR** (which may complicate acute MI) left atrial pressure is **markedly elevated** and cardiac output falls, the **left atrium is NOT enlarged**, and the patient presents with **acute pulmonary oedema** needing **urgent surgical repair or replacement**; in chronic compensated MR left atrial pressure is normal or mildly elevated with preserved forward output.

Markers of **severe mitral regurgitation** are a **soft S1, S3, widely split S2, displaced apex, mid-diastolic flow murmur** and signs of **pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary congestion**; the **loudness of the murmur does not reflect severity**.
**Mitral regurgitation** may present with **left- or right-sided heart failure**, **low-output symptoms, palpitation** or **infective endocarditis**.

In **severe MR, vasodilators and loop diuretics** are indicated only in **symptomatic patients who are not surgical candidates or as a bridge to surgery**, not in asymptomatic patients; **balloon dilatation has no role**. Surgery is indicated for **symptomatic patients, LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF below 60%), new-onset AF, pulmonary hypertension (PASP over 50 mmHg)** or moderate/severe secondary MR at the time of CABG; an elderly patient with a **heavily calcified valve** receives a **bioprosthetic valve replacement**.

**Mitral valve prolapse** presents in a young, anxious patient with **palpitation and non-exertional infra-mammary chest pain**, with a **mid-systolic (non-ejection) click and a late systolic murmur** that **increases with Valsalva**.

topics.n: Aortic and tricuspid disease, prosthetic valves

facts.t: Aetiologies of **aortic stenosis** are **rheumatic heart disease**, **degenerative calcific (sclerocalcific) disease in the elderly** and **bicuspid aortic valve**, which is a **common** cause and the **commonest congenital** cause; **Marfan syndrome does not cause aortic stenosis**.

**Severe aortic stenosis** presents with the triad of **exertional chest pain (angina), syncope and heart failure**, and **mortality rises sharply once symptoms start**: untreated survival is about **5 years with angina, 3 years with syncope and 2 years with heart failure**.

The main treatment of **symptomatic severe aortic stenosis** is **surgical aortic valve replacement**; replacement is also indicated in **asymptomatic severe AS with poor LV function** or when the patient is **undergoing CABG**, but not for asymptomatic severe AS alone. **Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)** is indicated for **high-risk patients for conventional surgery**.

**Aortic regurgitation** is caused by rheumatic fever and by **Marfan syndrome** (dilated ascending aorta), **congenital bicuspid valve**, infective endocarditis, syphilitic aortitis, severe hypertension, ankylosing spondylitis and aortic dissection; medical treatment is started with **vasodilators (e.g. ACE inhibitors)** to reduce regurgitant volume.

**Functional tricuspid regurgitation** (e.g. secondary to **severe mitral stenosis** with pulmonary hypertension) is **more common than primary** TR; the murmur **increases with inspiration and leg raising** and decreases on standing, the JVP shows **systolic expansion**, and long-standing severe TR causes **cachexia and jaundice**. Primary tricuspid disease may follow **carcinoid syndrome** or **intravenous drug use**.

Patients with a **mechanical mitral valve prosthesis** need **lifelong warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist)**; **direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated** and switching to rivaroxaban is not safe even in sinus rhythm. Valve choice is age-related: **bioprostheses suit elderly** patients, while mechanical valves are preferred in the young.

In **infective endocarditis**, check for **fever, clubbing, splenomegaly and a new murmur**, together with peripheral stigmata: **Osler nodes** (painful raised lesions on hands and feet), **splinter haemorrhages** and clubbing.

**Echocardiographic evidence** of endocarditis is a **major Duke criterion** (a single positive blood culture, fever and embolic manifestations are not). In an **intravenous drug user**, suspect **right-sided (tricuspid) methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus** endocarditis. **Antibiotic prophylaxis** for predisposed patients is indicated **before dental procedures**, not before hernioplasty, cataract surgery or colonoscopy.

**Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** is usually **autosomal dominant**, shows **marked septal hypertrophy**, and is a **common cause of sudden death in young subjects under 35 years**; exertional syncope in a young athlete should prompt exclusion of HCM.

An **atrial septal defect** causes a **right ventricular (diffuse) impulse** with a parasternal heave rather than a hyperdynamic left ventricular apex, while **coeur en sabot** (boot-shaped heart) on chest X-ray is the sign of **tetralogy of Fallot**, not of mitral regurgitation.

**Acute pericarditis** causes retrosternal chest pain lasting days that is **worse lying down and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward**, does not change with exertion, and often follows a **viral upper respiratory infection**.

The ECG in **acute pericarditis** shows **diffuse concave-upward ST elevation with diffuse PR-segment depression**; **convex ST elevation with reciprocal ST depression** indicates **STEMI**, not pericarditis.

**Cardiac tamponade** presents with **Beck triad**: **hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and distant (muffled) heart sounds**, plus **pulsus paradoxus** and **sinus tachycardia** as an early sign (not bradycardia); the **lungs are clear without pulmonary congestion**, the ECG may show **electrical alternans**, and the chest X-ray shows a **flask-shaped cardiac silhouette**. **Failure to show a pericardial effusion on echocardiography** makes tamponade unlikely.

**Pericardiocentesis is the life-saving treatment** of cardiac tamponade; **diuretics and inotropes are not** the main line of therapy. Tamponade may follow **coronary perforation during PCI** and may complicate **systemic lupus erythematosus**.
**Raised JVP with hypotension** occurs in both **cardiac tamponade and right ventricular myocardial infarction**.

**Constrictive pericarditis** shows **tachycardia** (not bradycardia; atrial fibrillation occurs in about a third), a small-volume pulse, **pulsus paradoxus**, a raised JVP with **Kussmaul sign** and prominent **x and y descents**, a **pericardial knock**, and **hepatomegaly with ascites**.

**Aortic dissection** presents with **severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back**, **unequal pulses and blood pressure between the arms**, an **early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation** (in Stanford **type A**, involving the ascending aorta) and sometimes a pericardial effusion; **Marfan syndrome** (tall stature, long extremities, hyperextensible joints) predisposes to dissection.

The main diagnostic modality for **aortic dissection** is **CT aortography (MSCT angiography)**; **hypertension is a risk factor**, and **Stanford type A dissection requires emergency surgery**, not medical management alone.

**Marfan syndrome** is **autosomal dominant** and is associated with **mitral valve prolapse, aortic regurgitation** (dilated aortic root) and **acute aortic dissection**, with **lens subluxation**; it does **not** cause aortic stenosis.

**Pulmonary hypertension (PH)** is most commonly caused by **left heart disease** (mitral valve disease causes **post-capillary PH**); other causes include **chest disease** and **Eisenmenger syndrome**. PH gives an **accentuated (loud) pulmonary component of S2**, a **palpable pulsation in the pulmonary area**, a **left parasternal heave** and **congested pulsating neck veins**.

**Pulmonary embolism (PE)** presents with **pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis and syncope**, with **sinus tachycardia** (not bradycardia), a loud P2, an **S1Q3T3 pattern** or atrial fibrillation on ECG, and blood gases showing **low PO2 and low PCO2**. Suspect PE with **recent surgery or immobility, malignancy, oral contraceptives** or **unilateral leg pain and swelling**; **bilateral fine basal rales** instead suggest left heart failure.

The definitive investigation for suspected **pulmonary embolism** is **CT pulmonary angiography**; start **low-molecular-weight heparin** while arranging it. **PE with shock** is treated with **thrombolytic therapy**.
**Transient loss of consciousness on standing** with a normal examination and no past history suggests **orthostatic hypotension** rather than a cardiac arrhythmia or valvular obstruction.

questions.q: Ordinary activity causes mild symptoms. In the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification this falls into which class?
e: NYHA II: slight limitation; comfortable at rest, ordinary activity causes symptoms.

questions.q: Less than ordinary activity causes symptoms. In the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification this falls into which class?
e: NYHA III: marked limitation; comfortable at rest but less-than-ordinary activity causes symptoms.

questions.q: Pulse in aortic regurge is usually:
e: Aortic regurgitation gives a large-volume (bounding, collapsing) pulse from big stroke volume and low diastolic pressure. Slow-rising/parvus et tardus belongs to aortic stenosis.

questions.q: All of the following statements are true EXCEPT:
o: A bounding pulse is specific only for aortic regurgitation
Pulsus alternans is defined by the beat-to-beat variability of the pulse amplitude
Pulsus parvus et tardus is best appreciated by careful palpation of the carotid arteries
A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg with inspiration is considered pathological
e: A bounding pulse also occurs in other high-output states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, PDA, fever), so it is not specific to AR. The other statements are true.

questions.q: All of the following statements are true EXCEPT:
o: A bounding pulse can occur in severe aortic regurgitation
Pulsus alternans is defined by the beat-to-beat variability of the pulse amplitude
Pulsus parvus et tardus is a sign of severe aortic stenosis
A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg with inspiration is considered physiological
e: Inspiratory fall in systolic BP up to 10 mmHg is physiological; >10 mmHg is pathological (pulsus paradoxus). So D is false.

questions.q: Pulsus parvus et tardus is a feature of which valvular disease?
e: Slow-rising, small-volume pulse (parvus et tardus) is the carotid sign of severe aortic stenosis due to fixed outflow obstruction.

questions.q: Pulsus paradoxus is a sign of:
e: Pulsus paradoxus is the classic sign of cardiac tamponade (also seen in constrictive pericarditis, severe asthma/COPD); pericarditis alone or HCM do not specifically cause it.

questions.q: Which of the following arterial pulse waveforms is consistent with severe left ventricular impairment?
e: Pulsus alternans (alternating strong/weak beats) signals severe LV systolic impairment.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding clinical examination are correct EXCEPT:
o: Pulsus paradoxus is a systolic pressure drop exceeding 10 mm Hg during expiration
Osler's nodes are painful, raised lesions found typically on the hands and feet in infective endocarditis
Central cyanosis is seen in warm as well as cold areas of the body during examination
Absent dorsalis pedis pulsations may be a normal variant
e: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggerated fall in systolic BP (>10 mmHg) during INSPIRATION, not expiration, so A is the incorrect statement.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding clinical examination findings are correct EXCEPT:
o: Pulsus paradoxus, an exaggerated inspiratory drop in systolic blood pressure, is a characteristic sign of severe aortic regurgitation
Osler's nodes are one of the classic immunologic peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis
Central cyanosis is best observed in warm areas like the tongue and buccal mucosa
Absence of dorsalis pedis pulsations can be a normal anatomical variant in a small percentage of the healthy population
e: Pulsus paradoxus characterises tamponade, not severe AR. The other statements are correct.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding blood pressure measurement is correct?
o: Korotkoff sounds are used to mark systolic and diastolic pressures
Auscultatory gap is a cause of underestimation of the systolic pressure
Unsupported arm might increase the measured values
e: All three statements are true: Korotkoff sounds define SBP/DBP; the auscultatory gap causes underestimation of SBP; an unsupported arm raises readings.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding blood pressure measurement are correct EXCEPT:
o: Korotkoff sounds are used to mark systolic and diastolic pressures
Auscultatory gap is a cause of underestimation of the systolic pressure
Unsupported arm might overestimate the measured values
Full urinary bladder might decrease the measured values
e: A full bladder INCREASES the reading (it does not lower it), so D is the incorrect statement.

questions.q: Regarding blood pressure measurement, all are true EXCEPT:
o: In AR we record both muffling and disappearance of sounds
Full bladder can cause incorrect readings of blood pressure
e: Korotkoff phase 5 is disappearance of sounds; phase 4 is muffling. So B is false.

questions.q: Diastolic blood pressure:
o: Is estimated by recording Phase 4 Korotkoff (muffling) sounds
Is estimated by recording Phase 5 Korotkoff (disappearance) sounds
Is estimated by recording Phase 5 Korotkoff (disappearance) sounds in patients with aortic regurge and in children
e: Diastolic BP is taken at phase 5 (disappearance). (In AR and children phase 4 and 5 are both recorded.)

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding general clinical examination is correct?
o: Mitral facies, characterized by mild cyanosis of the lips, cheeks, and malar prominences without finger clubbing, can be seen in patients with severe, long-standing mitral stenosis
Splinter hemorrhages under the nails are considered a classic peripheral sign of infective endocarditis
Clinical features suggestive of Marfan syndrome should prompt investigation for associated aortic root dilatation or aneurysm
e: Mitral facies, splinter haemorrhages and Marfan features (with aortic root dilatation risk) are all correct, so D.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding clinical examination are correct EXCEPT:
o: Malar rash could be seen in patients with severe mitral stenosis
Osler's nodes are one of the diagnostic criteria for rheumatic fever
Central cyanosis is seen in warm as well as cold areas of the body during examination
Xanthelasma palpebrarum could be seen in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia
e: Osler nodes are a sign of infective endocarditis, not a Jones criterion for rheumatic fever.

questions.q: Regarding the normal jugular venous pulse:
o: Has three positive waves "a", "c" and "v" waves
The "a" wave occurs just after the P wave of the ECG
e: The JVP has three positive waves (a, c, v); the a wave follows the P wave; the venous pulse collapses in systole (x descent). All true.

questions.q: All the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: The center of the right atrium lies approximately 5 cm below the sternal angle, which is used as the reference point
Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP) occurs in right ventricular failure, tricuspid stenosis, or tricuspid regurgitation
Raised JVP occurs in SVC obstruction
JVP increases during inspiration in normal individuals
e: JVP FALLS with inspiration in normal individuals (a rise is Kussmaul sign). So D is false.

questions.q: As regards neck veins, all are correct EXCEPT (recalled exception): the right atrium lies approximately 8 cm below the angle of Louis.
questions.sa: False statement: the centre of the right atrium is about 5 cm below the sternal angle (angle of Louis) at 45 degrees, not 8 cm; normal CVP < 7 cm H2O.
e: The right atrium lies about 5 cm below the sternal angle (angle of Louis), not 8 cm.

questions.q: A prominent "a" wave in the jugular venous pulse can be caused by:
e: A prominent a wave occurs when the RA contracts against resistance: RV hypertrophy, tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary stenosis/hypertension.

questions.q: "a" wave in the jugular venous waveform is absent in which of the following conditions?
e: No atrial contraction in AF, so the a wave is absent.

questions.q: Cannon waves in the jugular venous pulse can be caused by:
e: Cannon a waves occur when the atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve, e.g. in complete heart block with AV dissociation (atria and ventricles beat independently, so atrial systole sometimes falls on a closed valve).

questions.q: Systolic expansion of the neck veins can be caused by:
f: Keyed per Allam; other options (TR) also cause systolic expansion.
e: As keyed (Allam): in AF the a wave is lost and the neck veins show systolic expansion instead of the normal systolic collapse.

questions.q: In tricuspid regurgitation the JVP is raised with a prominent ___ wave (not an a wave).
questions.sa: Prominent V wave (systolic expansion of the neck veins); the giant a wave is a feature of TS/PS/pulmonary hypertension.
e: Tricuspid regurgitation gives a prominent v wave (systolic expansion of neck veins/pulsatile liver).

questions.q: You suspect atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis, if:
o: The first heart sound is accentuated
The opening snap is no longer heard
The neck veins show systolic expansion in the absence of significant tricuspid regurgitation
e: Systolic expansion of neck veins without significant TR suggests AF (loss of a wave, no x descent).

questions.q: A distressed patient is brought to the ER by ambulance. He is short of breath with a respiratory rate of 34 cycles/min and BP 120/82 mmHg. He has a rumbling diastolic murmur over the heart with presystolic accentuation. He has bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations over the lungs. If his heart rate was 136 beat/min and irregular, the jugular venous pressure will be:
o: Congested with a prominent a wave
e: Rapid irregular rate = AF: JVP is congested with systolic expansion (no a wave, no systolic collapse).

questions.q: Kussmaul's sign: what happens to the JVP during inspiration?
questions.sa: Paradoxical rise (inspiratory filling) of the JVP during inspiration; seen in constrictive pericarditis (absent in tamponade, IM PDF 67).
e: Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical RISE of JVP on inspiration, seen in constrictive pericarditis (absent in tamponade).

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct?
o: Clubbing is common in patients with heart failure
Patent foramen ovale is a common etiology of clubbing
e: Clubbing is associated with cyanotic congenital disease (right-to-left shunt) and infective endocarditis; it is not common in heart failure or PFO, and is not simply reversible in all cases.

questions.q: All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: The normal apex impulse, localized within the midclavicular line, lasts more than two-thirds of systole.
A dilated right ventricle could cause a left parasternal impulse.
Mitral stenosis could cause a palpable first heart sound.
Right ventricular enlargement causes a diffuse apical impulse.
e: A normal apex impulse is localized and lasts less than two-thirds of systole; A is the false statement.

questions.q: All are true EXCEPT:
o: In MS the apex is tapping (slapping).
In MR the apex is hyperdynamic.
In AR the apex is heaving.
e: In AR the apex is hyperdynamic (volume overload, displaced); heaving is for pressure overload (AS, hypertension).

questions.q: All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Severe aortic stenosis causes a heaving apex.
Severe aortic regurgitation causes a hyperdynamic apex.
Severe isolated mitral stenosis causes the apex to shift downwards.
Right ventricular enlargement causes a diffuse apical impulse.
e: Isolated MS does not enlarge the LV, so the apex is not displaced downwards (tapping apex, in normal position).

questions.q: A distressed patient is brought to the ER by ambulance. He is short of breath with a respiratory rate of 34 cycles/min and BP 120/40 mmHg. He has a long-standing early diastolic murmur over the second aortic area. He has bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations over the lungs. The apex of the heart will be:
o: In the left 5th space MCL, localized, with systolic bulge and sustained.
In the left 6th space AAL, diffuse, with systolic bulge and sustained (heaving).
In the left 6th space AAL, localized, with systolic bulge and hyperkinetic.
In the left 5th space AAL, diffuse, with systolic retraction.
e: Severe AR: volume-loaded LV gives a displaced (6th space AAL), localized, hyperkinetic apex with systolic bulge.

questions.q: All the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Mitral valve closure is the main component of the first heart sound.
Reversed splitting of the second heart sound may occur in severe aortic stenosis.
The third heart sound is a high-pitched sound occurring in early systole.
The fourth heart sound occurs in late diastole.
e: S3 is a LOW-pitched sound in EARLY DIASTOLE (rapid filling), not high-pitched early systole.

questions.q: All the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Mitral stenosis usually causes a muffled first heart sound.
A muffled second heart sound may occur in severe aortic stenosis.
The third heart sound occurs in early diastole.
The fourth heart sound occurs with the atrial contraction phase.
e: Mitral stenosis gives an ACCENTUATED (loud, snapping) S1 while the valve is pliable; muffled S1 occurs when calcified.

questions.q: All the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Mitral valve closure is the main component of the first heart sound.
Reversed splitting of the second heart sound may occur in severe aortic stenosis.
A fourth heart sound might be normal in children.
A fourth heart sound could be appreciated in patients with uncontrolled systemic hypertension.
e: S3 (not S4) can be physiological in children/young adults; S4 is always abnormal.

questions.q: Regarding heart sounds, which of the following is TRUE?
o: A loud S1 is expected in severe mitral regurgitation due to forceful valve closure.
A fixed splitting of S2 is characteristic of severe aortic stenosis.
An opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex is a classic auscultatory finding in mitral stenosis with a pliable valve.
The third heart sound (S3) is always pathological regardless of the patient's age.
e: Opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble = MS with a pliable valve. MR has a soft S1; AS gives single/paradoxical S2; S3 may be normal in the young.

questions.q: Which heart sound is lost in atrial fibrillation?
e: S4 requires effective atrial contraction, so it is lost in AF.

questions.q: An additional heart sound heard just before S1 (late diastolic/presystolic) in a patient with aortic stenosis is:
questions.sa: Fourth heart sound (S4) - late diastolic (presystolic), due to forced atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle (AS = tension overload); also listed over the mitral area in AS (Allam 70).
e: Presystolic/late-diastolic sound = S4, from forceful atrial contraction against a stiff hypertrophied LV.

questions.q: The opening snap of mitral stenosis is absent when the mitral valve is:
questions.sa: Calcified (heavily calcified/rigid valve) - the opening snap denotes a non-calcified, pliable valve; its absence suggests calcific MS (Allam 62, 67).
e: The opening snap needs a pliable valve; it disappears when the valve is heavily calcified/immobile.

questions.q: A 29-year-old female patient on long-acting penicillin presents to the clinic with palpitation; on examination there is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla with a muffled S1 (mitral regurgitation). Another physician noticed prominent pulsations and accentuation of S2 in the left second intercostal space (pulmonary area); this is mostly related to:
e: Prominent pulmonary-area pulsation with loud P2 indicates pulmonary hypertension (secondary to mitral disease).

questions.q: The murmur of pulmonary regurgitation (a right-sided murmur) increases in intensity with:
questions.sa: Inspiration (Carvallo's sign) - right-sided murmurs are louder on inspiration; left-sided murmurs louder on expiration.
e: Right-sided murmurs increase on inspiration (Carvallo sign).

questions.q: A soft blowing pansystolic murmur heard over the cardiac apex, propagating to the axilla but not to the neck, and which does not increase in intensity with inspiration, can be due to:
e: A soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla and not increasing with inspiration is MR (TR increases with inspiration; VSD is at the left sternal edge).

questions.q: An apical pansystolic murmur propagating to the base of the heart but not to the carotids, and not increasing in intensity with inspiration, can be due to:
o: Calcific senile severe aortic valve stenosis
e: Posterior leaflet prolapse gives an anteriorly directed jet that radiates to the base but not to the carotids; AS murmur is ejection and radiates to carotids.

questions.q: Each of the following statements regarding the auscultatory findings of mitral regurgitation is correct EXCEPT:
o: Pansystolic murmur over the apex propagated to the axilla.
Third heart sound over the apex.
Systolic ejection murmur propagated to the base of the heart.
e: MR: muffled S1, pansystolic apical murmur to axilla, S3. An ejection systolic murmur to the base is not typical.

questions.q: Auscultatory findings in a patient with severe mitral stenosis include:
o: Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with presystolic accentuation.
Loud aortic component of the second heart sound.
Ejection systolic click over the apex.
e: Severe MS: mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation (if sinus rhythm), loud S1, opening snap, loud P2 if PH.

questions.q: Signs of severe mitral stenosis include:
o: An opening snap close to the second heart sound.
Loud aortic component of the second heart sound.
An opening snap close to the first heart sound.
e: In severe MS the opening snap is close to S2 (high left atrial pressure opens the valve early).

questions.q: Auscultatory findings in a patient with severe calcific aortic stenosis include:
o: Loud aortic component of the second heart sound.
Wide splitting of the second heart sound.
Soft holosystolic murmur over the cardiac apex.
Late-peaking systolic ejection murmur over the aortic area propagating to the carotids.
e: Calcific AS: late-peaking ejection systolic murmur to the carotids, soft/absent A2 and single or paradoxically split S2.

questions.q: On auscultation of the second aortic area, the aortic regurgitation murmur is characterised by:
e: AR murmur is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the aortic area/left sternal edge.

questions.q: Concerning severe aortic regurgitation:
o: All aortic valve murmurs are heard best with the patient on their left side with the breath held in end-expiration.
It causes a 'water-hammer' character in the radial pulse.
It causes an 'ejection systolic' murmur as its characteristic murmur.
It causes a pansystolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
e: Severe AR causes a wide pulse pressure with rapid diastolic runoff into the LV, producing a water-hammer (collapsing) pulse. Its characteristic murmur is early diastolic decrescendo, not ejection systolic or pansystolic.

questions.q: The diastolic murmur of Austin Flint:
o: Is associated with a loud first heart sound.
Is an early sign of aortic regurgitation.
Can be distinguished from the murmur of mitral stenosis by the absence of presystolic accentuation.
Is due to partial closure of the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve.
e: Austin Flint murmur is mid-diastolic and, unlike MS, has no presystolic accentuation and no loud S1/opening snap.

questions.q: All the following statements about the diastolic murmur of Austin Flint are correct EXCEPT:
o: It is not associated with a loud first heart sound.
It is a sign of mild aortic regurgitation.
It can be distinguished from the murmur of mitral stenosis by the absence of presystolic accentuation.
It is due to partial closure of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve by the regurgitant aortic jet.
e: Austin Flint murmur indicates SEVERE AR (jet impinges on the anterior mitral leaflet), so B is false.

questions.q: An Austin Flint murmur:
o: Is always associated with a loud first heart sound.
Is always associated with a loud second heart sound.
Is due to encroachment of the aortic regurgitant jet on the posterior mitral valve leaflet.
e: Austin Flint murmur is a mid-diastolic apical murmur of functional mitral stenosis: the severe AR jet impinges on the anterior mitral leaflet and partially closes it. Unlike true MS it has no loud S1, no opening snap and no presystolic accentuation.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding cardiac apex examination are correct EXCEPT:
o: Aortic stenosis causes a heaving apex
Aortic regurgitation causes a hyperdynamic apex
Atrial septal defect causes a hyperdynamic apex
Right ventricular enlargement causes a diffuse apex
e: ASD causes a right ventricular (diffuse) impulse/parasternal heave, not a hyperdynamic LV apex.

questions.q: All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Severe mitral stenosis with marked calcification could be associated with a weak first heart sound.
Complete right bundle branch block causes the second heart sound to split widely.
Pulmonary stenosis causes a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound.
An opening snap close to the second heart sound is a sign of severity of mitral stenosis.
e: Pulmonary stenosis makes the pulmonary component of S2 soft/delayed, not loud.

questions.q: All the following sentences are true EXCEPT:
o: Marked pulse irregularity is a sign of atrial fibrillation
Ejection systolic murmur over the aortic area is suggestive of aortic stenosis
Mitral regurge is commonly associated with a loud S1
Neck veins examination is reliable in assessing the fluid status of patients
e: MR is associated with a soft/muffled S1; a loud S1 suggests MS.

questions.q: A 50 year old man has reversed splitting of the second heart sound on examination. Which of the following conditions shows this finding?
e: Reversed (paradoxical) splitting occurs with delayed LV emptying: severe AS (also LBBB).

questions.q: Which of the following is correct regarding the third heart sound?
o: It occurs during the atrial contraction phase
It occurs during passive left ventricular filling
It is a common physiological finding in adults
It is lost with atrial fibrillation
e: S3 is produced by rapid passive LV filling in early diastole.

questions.q: Which additional heart sound might be normal in children?
e: S3 can be physiological in children and young adults.

questions.q: All the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Mitral stenosis usually causes an accentuated first heart sound.
Valvular aortic stenosis causes a muffled second heart sound.
Third heart sound occurs in late diastole.
The fourth heart sound could reflect a stiff left ventricle.
e: S3 occurs in EARLY diastole, so C is wrong.

questions.q: All the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Rheumatic mitral stenosis usually causes an accentuated first heart sound.
Severe aortic stenosis usually causes an accentuated second heart sound.
Third heart sound occurs in early diastole.
The fourth heart sound occurs with the atrial contraction phase.
e: Severe AS causes a soft/muffled A2, not accentuated.

questions.q: Which of the following is responsible for the fourth heart sound?
e: S4 is produced by atrial systole forcing blood into a stiff ventricle.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the auscultatory finding of a fourth heart sound (S4) on physical examination?
o: A hallmark of the onset of atrial fibrillation
e: S4 is classically associated with hypertension (LVH, stiff LV).

questions.q: Which of the following auscultatory findings is never found on physical examination in a patient with atrial fibrillation?
o: Inspiratory splitting of the second heart sound
e: S4 needs atrial contraction, so it is never present in AF.

questions.q: A 74 year old woman presented to you complaining of exertional dizziness. Cardiac auscultation revealed an ejection systolic murmur over the base of the heart propagating to the carotids with an extra sound heard shortly before the first heart sound. Which of the following is a possible cause of that sound?
e: Pre-S1 sound in a patient with AS and LVH = S4.

questions.q: A 64 year old hypertensive man is noted on auscultation to have an extra sound shortly before the first heart sound. Which of the following is a possible cause of that sound?
e: Pre-S1 sound in a hypertensive man = S4.

questions.q: A 22 year old woman presented to you complaining of exertional shortness of breath. Cardiac auscultation revealed a pan-systolic murmur over the apex propagating to the axilla with an extra sound heard shortly after the second heart sound. Which of the following is a possible cause of that sound?
e: Extra sound just after S2 in MR = S3 (rapid filling of a volume-loaded ventricle).

questions.q: A 24 year old female, complaining of atypical chest pain and palpitation. She is noted to have an extra sound shortly after the first heart sound. Which of the following is a possible cause of that sound?
e: Extra sound shortly after S1 in a young woman with atypical chest pain suggests mitral valve prolapse: non-ejection (mid-systolic) click.

questions.q: Auscultatory findings in a patient with severe mitral stenosis include all the following EXCEPT:
o: Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with presystolic accentuation.
Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound.
e: The opening snap occurs in early DIASTOLE, not systole.

questions.q: Auscultatory findings in a patient with severe mitral stenosis include all the following EXCEPT:
o: Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with presystolic accentuation.
Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound.
Wide second heart sound - opening snap time interval.
e: In severe MS the interval between S2 and the opening snap is NARROW, not wide.

questions.q: In mitral stenosis, a narrow time interval between the second heart sound and an opening snap indicates:
e: High LA pressure in severe MS opens the valve early, giving a short S2-OS interval.

questions.q: The auscultatory findings of isolated mitral stenosis include:
o: Soft early diastolic murmur heard all over the precordium with maximum intensity over the second aortic area.
Opening snap over the left parasternal border.
Third heart sound over the apex.
e: Isolated MS: loud S1, opening snap at the left sternal edge/apex, mid-diastolic rumble. Soft early diastolic murmur is AR.

questions.q: A patient presents with an early diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border. Which of the following is most likely to produce this diastolic murmur?
o: Mitral valve stenosis with atrial fibrillation
e: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border = aortic regurgitation.

questions.q: Each of the following statements regarding mitral regurgitation is true EXCEPT:
o: Pansystolic murmur over the apex propagated to the axilla
Systolic ejection murmur propagating to the base of the heart
e: MR does not produce an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the base; its murmur is pansystolic to the axilla.

questions.q: The following statement regarding the auscultatory findings in tricuspid regurge is correct:
o: Pansystolic murmur over the left parasternal area that increases with inspiration.
Pansystolic murmur over the apex propagating to the axilla.
Fourth heart sound over the left parasternal area.
Systolic ejection murmur propagating to the base of the heart.
e: TR: pansystolic murmur at the left parasternal area, louder on inspiration.

questions.q: Concerning pulmonary valve stenosis:
o: All pulmonary valve murmurs are heard best with the patient on their left side with breath held in end expiration
It causes an 'ejection systolic' murmur which increases with inspiration.
It causes an 'ejection systolic' murmur which doesn't change with inspiration.
It causes a pan-systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
e: Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur louder on inspiration (right-sided).

questions.q: The murmur of aortic stenosis is characterised by all the following EXCEPT:
o: Late peaking is related to severity
Best heard over the aortic area
e: AS murmur is an ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur, not pansystolic rumbling.

questions.q: Which statement is correct regarding the clinical findings in severe aortic stenosis?
o: Accentuated aortic component of the second heart sound
Wide fixed splitting of the second heart sound
Pansystolic murmur propagated to the base.
e: Pulsus parvus et tardus is a sign of severe AS; A2 is soft and splitting is paradoxical, not fixed.

questions.q: Auscultatory findings in a patient with severe calcific aortic stenosis include all the following EXCEPT:
o: Weak aortic component of the second heart sound.
Wide splitting of the second heart sound.
Late-peaking systolic ejection murmur over the aortic area propagating to the carotids.
e: Severe calcific AS gives a single or paradoxically split S2, not wide splitting.

questions.q: Auscultatory findings in a patient with severe calcific aortic stenosis include all the following EXCEPT:
o: Weak aortic component of the second heart sound.
Paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound.
Early-peaking systolic ejection murmur over the aortic area propagating to the carotids.
e: Severe AS murmur is LATE-peaking, not early-peaking.

questions.q: The systolic murmur of sub-valvular aortic stenosis:
o: Is associated with a loud first heart sound.
Is associated with an ejection click.
Is an ejection murmur, best heard in the second aortic area.
Is due to partial closure of the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve.
e: Subvalvular AS gives an ejection murmur at the aortic area without an ejection click.

questions.q: In a patient with known severe aortic regurgitation, auscultation reveals a loud early diastolic murmur in the aortic area. You also hear a quiet mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. This is:
o: Austin Flint murmur of functional mitral stenosis.
e: Mid-diastolic apical murmur in severe AR is the Austin Flint murmur (functional MS).

questions.q: Which of the following cardiac lesions is NOT associated with a systolic murmur?
f: Ambiguous: Eisenmenger PDA may have no murmur.
Answer key added: I (source Q082 keys I, 'None of the above'; the published bank had no key).
e: As keyed in the source: every listed lesion is associated with a systolic murmur (AS/PS ejection murmurs; MVP/HOCM systolic murmurs; ASD pulmonary flow murmur; TR/VSD pansystolic murmurs), so 'none of the above' is the answer. Teaching caveat: in Eisenmenger PDA the classic continuous murmur disappears once pulmonary pressures equal systemic pressures, which is why this question is often doubted — the key follows the source.

questions.q: Regarding dynamic auscultation, sustained isometric handgrip increases the murmur intensity of all the following EXCEPT:
e: Handgrip increases afterload: AR, MR and VSD murmurs increase, while AS (and HOCM) murmurs decrease. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: What is the name given to the propagation of the aortic stenosis murmur to the apex?
questions.sa: Gallavardin phenomenon (sign): the high-frequency component of the AS ejection murmur radiates to the apex, where it may mimic mitral regurgitation.
e: Gallavardin phenomenon: AS murmur radiating to the apex and mimicking MR.

questions.q: (Follows the preceding case on the same paper: a 29-year-old female on long-acting penicillin presenting with palpitation; a pansystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla with muffled S1 = rheumatic mitral regurgitation.) Another physician noticed prominent pulsations and accentuation of S2 in the second intercostal space. This is mostly related to:
e: See Q040: loud, palpable P2 means pulmonary hypertension. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: Select the correct cardiac axis shown in this ECG:
e: QRS predominantly negative in aVF/II and positive in lead I: left axis deviation.

questions.q: Select the correct cardiac axis shown in this ECG:
e: Dominant negative lead I with positive inferior leads: right axis deviation.

questions.q: Which of the following is correct regarding this ECG?
e: Lead I positive, lead aVF/III negative: left axis deviation, without wide QRS (no LBBB/RBBB).

questions.q: 55-year-old male patient, smoker, hypertensive, with severe central chest pain radiating to his shoulders, associated with nausea; he is vitally stable. His ECG is shown. Can you determine the axis of this ECG?
e: Positive lead I with negative aVF: left axis.

questions.q: ECG tracing (lead II) shown. The abnormality present in this tracing can be a clue to:
e: Prominent, broad notched P wave (P mitrale) in lead II is a clue to mitral stenosis.

questions.q: The following ECG shows:
o: A pattern of left bundle branch block
e: Tall R in left leads and deep S in right precordial leads: LVH.

questions.q: The following ECG reveals:
o: A pattern of right bundle branch block
e: High voltage with ST depression/T inversion in lateral leads: LVH with strain.

questions.q: Select the correct answer for this ECG:
e: High QRS voltage with ST depression/T-wave inversion in the lateral leads — the strain pattern of LVH. LBBB requires a wide QRS with broad monophasic R laterally, and recent posterior MI gives tall R waves in V1–V2; the voltage-plus-strain combination is LVH with strain.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: LVH voltage criteria plus ST depression and T-wave inversion in the lateral leads: the strain pattern — a repolarization abnormality of the hypertrophied ventricle — so LVH with strain, not LVH alone or NSTEMI.

questions.q: Select the correct diagnosis of this ECG:
e: High-voltage left-sided complexes: LVH.

questions.q: This ECG can be found in which of the following diseases?
e: LVH voltage as in systemic hypertension, not RV pattern.

questions.q: The following ECG shows:
o: A pattern of right bundle branch block
e: Dominant R in V1 with right axis: RVH.

questions.q: This ECG shows:
e: The tracing satisfies none of the three listed patterns — no wide-QRS bundle branch block morphology and no LVH voltage criteria — so 'none of the above' is the answer.

questions.q: This ECG can be found in which of the following diseases?
e: Right-sided hypertrophy pattern, seen in severe pulmonary stenosis.

questions.q: This ECG can be detected in the following diseases EXCEPT:
e: RVH pattern occurs in PS, tight MS and primary PH, not isolated AS (LVH).

questions.q: Select the correct diagnosis of this ECG:
e: Tall R in V1 with right axis: RVH.

questions.q: What would you do to confirm the finding in this ECG?
o: Repeat the ECG after few hours
e: Voltage criteria are only suggestive; echocardiography confirms hypertrophy.

questions.q: The following ECG shows:
o: A pattern of left bundle branch block
e: Wide QRS with broad notched R in lateral leads and deep S in V1-V3: LBBB.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: Broad QRS with deep S V1-V3 and discordant ST-T: LBBB.

questions.q: The following ECG shows:
o: A pattern of right bundle branch block
e: rSR' in V1 with wide QRS: RBBB.

questions.q: This ECG shows:
e: RSR' in right precordial leads with wide S in lateral leads: RBBB.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: RSR' in V1 with wide QRS: RBBB.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: RSR' (M-shaped) complex in V1 with a wide QRS and broad S waves in the lateral leads: right bundle branch block.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: Normal tracing: normal axis, narrow QRS, no ST changes.

questions.q: Select the correct answer for this ECG:
e: Tall peaked T waves with widened QRS: hyperkalaemia.

questions.q: A 55-year-old heavy smoker presents with dyspnea on walking 300 meters; examination shows a displaced apex and jugular venous distension. CXR shows cardiomegaly and the ECG is normal apart from sinus tachycardia. The investigation of choice in this situation is:
e: Dyspnoea, displaced apex, JVD and cardiomegaly suggest cardiac disease; echocardiography is the investigation of choice.

questions.q: Exercise ECG is one of the exercise testing modalities; it is usually used for assessment of ECG changes with exercise in which group of patients?
o: Patients suspected to have rheumatic heart disease
Patients with suspected coronary artery disease
To delineate coronary anatomy in known ischemic patients
e: Exercise (stress) ECG provokes ischemia during exertion — typically ST depression — in patients with suspected coronary artery disease whose resting ECG may be normal; it assesses ECG changes with exercise, not coronary anatomy.

questions.q: All of the following lines can be used in the evaluation of patients with chest pain:
e: All three are used in chest-pain evaluation: exercise ECG as provocative/functional testing, thallium-201 imaging for perfusion defects, and coronary angiography to define coronary anatomy.

questions.q: Holter monitoring is 24-hour monitoring of the ECG; it can be used for the following indications:
o: Patients with recurrent attacks of syncope
Recurrent palpitations with no available data from the resting ECG
e: Holter monitoring suits syncope and unexplained recurrent palpitations.

questions.q: The QRS complex duration:
o: Is between 100 and 120 msec in incomplete bundle branch block.
Is more than 120 msec in complete bundle branch block.
e: Normal QRS duration is <120 ms (usually <100 ms); 100–120 ms is incomplete bundle branch block and >120 ms is complete bundle branch block — all three statements hold.

questions.q: All the following statements regarding the normal P wave are correct EXCEPT:
o: Is less than 120 msec in duration.
Is more than 2.5 mm in amplitude.
e: Normal P wave is <2.5 mm, so D is false.

questions.q: In case of right atrial enlargement, the P wave of the ECG is:
e: Right atrial enlargement gives a tall peaked P (>2.5 mm, P pulmonale) with normal duration.

questions.q: The normal PR interval of the ECG:
o: Is measured from the beginning of the P wave to the end of the QRS complex.
Represents the time it takes for the stimulus to spread through the atria and pass through the AV junction.
Is less than 120 msec in duration.
e: The PR interval is the time for the impulse to spread through the atria and pass through the AV junction — measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS.

questions.q: The normal PR interval in the ECG:
o: Is the interval measured between the end of the P wave and the beginning of the QRS.
Is the interval measured between the beginning of the P wave and the beginning of the QRS.
e: PR runs from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of QRS (normal 120-200 ms).

questions.q: The PR interval in the ECG represents:
o: Time interval for atrial depolarization and repolarization.
Time interval from initial stimulation of the atria to initial stimulation of the ventricles.
Time interval from end of stimulation of the atria to initial stimulation of the ventricles.
e: PR interval = time from initial atrial to initial ventricular activation.

questions.q: On the horizontal axis of the ECG paper, each millimeter (small square) represents:
e: One small square on the horizontal axis = 0.04 s at 25 mm/s.

questions.q: The normal P wave in the ECG:
o: Is always negative in lead II.
Is always positive in lead aVR.
Denotes repolarization of the two atria.
May be biphasic in lead V1.
e: P wave may be biphasic in V1; it is positive in II and negative in aVR.

questions.q: The normal P wave:
o: Is between 120 msec and 150 msec in duration.
Is more than 2.5 mm in amplitude.
e: Normal P is positive in II, negative in aVR, <120 ms, <2.5 mm.

questions.q: The chest lead V2 of the ECG is located over the anterior chest:
o: In the fourth intercostal space just to the right of the sternum
In the fourth intercostal space just to the left of the sternum
In the fifth intercostal space just to the right of the sternum
e: V2: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: CT coronary angiography is contraindicated in which condition?
e: Iodinated contrast makes CT coronary angiography undesirable in chronic kidney disease. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: The following is an indication for electrophysiology (EP) study:
e: EP studies guide ablation of accessory pathways and assess SVT. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: A 45-year-old female with a history of rheumatic heart disease presents with palpitation. Her rhythm strip is shown. The patient's rhythm strip is showing:
e: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: A patient with an irregular pulse; his ECG shows:
e: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals without P waves: AF.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female with a history of rheumatic heart disease presents with palpitation. Her rhythm strip shows atrial fibrillation (see image). Which management lines are most appropriate in this case?
e: AF with rheumatic MS: rate control (beta-blocker) plus warfarin anticoagulation (DOACs are not used in rheumatic MS).

questions.q: This is the ECG of a 45-year-old patient with a history of rheumatic heart disease and moderate mitral stenosis, who recently suffers from palpitation and dizziness for 5 days. What is your recommended line of treatment?
e: AF with moderate MS: rate control with a beta-blocker and anticoagulation to prevent embolism.

questions.q: A 69-year-old male undergoes successful CABG and aortic valve replacement. On the 5th post-operative day he complains of palpitation, shortness of breath, fatigue and chest tightness. His BP is 70/30, HR 140/min and RR 30/min. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral basal crackles. An ECG rhythm strip is obtained. Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient?
e: AF with RVR and hypotension/pulmonary congestion is unstable: synchronized DC cardioversion.

questions.q: An unresponsive patient is brought to the ER by ambulance. He is in ventricular tachycardia with a heart rate of 210 beats/min and BP 70/40 mmHg. The first step in treatment is to:
e: Unstable VT — unresponsive with hypotension (70/40): immediate synchronized DC cardioversion. Drugs have no role in unstable VT; adenosine is for stable SVT, not VT.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents to the ER arrested; this is his rhythm strip. Which of the following best fits?
o: Disregard the ECG finding, continue basic life support
Direct current cardioversion immediately, it is ventricular tachycardia
e: Regular wide-complex tachycardia in an arrested patient = VT; unsynchronized/immediate DC shock.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of the second part of this rhythm strip:
e: Second part shows a changing-amplitude twisting wide-complex tachycardia: polymorphic VT.

questions.q: A 77-year-old male is admitted to the hospital with chest pain. He is known to have significant stable angina for which he takes aspirin and nitrates. Five hours after admission he begins to feel lightheaded and exhausted. His BP is 100/60 mmHg. An urgent ECG is obtained and a rhythm strip is shown below. Which of the following is the best next step in managing this patient?
e: Long pause with failure of AV/SA conduction in a symptomatic patient: pacemaker insertion.

questions.q: An 80-year-old female patient presents with recurrent attacks of syncope. Her ECG is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
o: Second degree Mobitz type 1 heart block
Second degree Mobitz type 2 heart block
e: P waves and QRS complexes dissociated, slow ventricular rate in an elderly woman with syncope: complete heart block.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man with a past medical history of cancer bladder and hematuria presents to the ER after an attack of loss of consciousness for 7-10 min during micturition in the standing position. This rhythm strip is recorded at the time of admission. Which of the following most likely accounts for the recorded ECG changes?
e: Dropped beats with intact P waves: AV conduction impairment (vagal/Mobitz) after micturition.

questions.q: A 25-year-old asymptomatic tennis player (ECG rhythm strip shown). The heart rate in this strip is:
e: R-R about 6 large squares: 300/6 = 50/min.

questions.q: A routine ECG of a 28-year-old tennis player shows:
e: Regular slow rhythm with normal P-QRS in an athlete: sinus bradycardia.

questions.q: The following ECG shows:
e: Saw-tooth flutter waves: atrial flutter.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate diagnosis:
e: Regular narrow tachycardia with flutter waves (2:1 block): atrial flutter.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
e: Flutter waves with irregular ventricular response: atrial flutter with variable block.

questions.q: Select the correct answer:
e: Rapid regular narrow-complex rhythm, no visible sinus P waves: SVT.

questions.q: This ECG is consistent with the diagnosis of:
e: Short PR with delta wave: Wolff-Parkinson-White.

questions.q: What is the rhythm?
e: Regular narrow rhythm with no sinus P waves at about 60-100/min: accelerated junctional rhythm.

questions.q: Select the proper answer:
o: Sinus tachycardia with premature ventricular contraction
e: Sinus tachycardia with a wide premature beat: PVC.
