questions.q: Can you tell the heart rate of this rhythm strip?
e: About 2.3 large squares between R waves: 300/2.3, about 130/min.

questions.q: Calculate the heart rate of this ECG. (Since the R-R intervals are equal: HR = 300 / R-R interval in large boxes, or HR = 1500 / R-R interval in small boxes.)
e: Rate = 300 / (R-R in large squares): about 100-105/min.

questions.q: A 33-year-old female with rheumatic heart disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, non-compliant with treatment, presents with recent left-sided hemiplegia. Cardiac examination reveals an accentuated S1, an apical mid-diastolic rumbling murmur, and an accentuated P2. Discontinuation of which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the recurrence of her arrhythmia?
f: Wording: warfarin withdrawal explains the stroke, digoxin the rate; keyed answer kept.
e: Digoxin slows AV-nodal conduction and controls the ventricular rate in AF; stopping it lets the rate escape and the paroxysmal AF recur. Warfarin withdrawal explains the embolic stroke (left-sided hemiplegia from a left atrial clot in rheumatic MS), not the recurrence of the arrhythmia.

questions.q: The following ECG reveals which abnormal rhythm?
e: Irregularly irregular without P waves: AF.

questions.q: Select the correct rhythm:
e: Irregular R-R with fibrillatory baseline: AF.

questions.q: Select the correct rhythm:
e: Irregular R-R, no P waves: AF.

questions.q: Select the correct rhythm:
e: Irregular R-R, no P waves: AF.

questions.q: A 53-year-old male is admitted to the hospital with a 2-week history of fatigue, dyspnea and decrease in effort tolerance. His BP is 150/90 and HR is 130/min. Lungs are clear on auscultation. Echocardiography shows a dilated LV with EF of 35% and moderate mitral regurgitation. A rhythm strip of lead II shows: Which of the following will be the first recommended intervention?
e: AF with fast rate and tachycardia-related LV dysfunction: first control rate/rhythm.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female patient presenting with sudden onset of rapid palpitation. Her BP is 90/60. She is dizzy with cold extremities. Her ECG shows: What is your next step?
e: Narrow regular tachycardia with hypotension and cold extremities = unstable SVT: DC cardioversion.

questions.q: A 75-year-old female patient presenting with sudden onset of rapid palpitation. Her BP is 90/60. She is dizzy with cold extremities. Her ECG shows: What is your next step?
e: Wide regular tachycardia with haemodynamic compromise = unstable VT: DC cardioversion.

questions.q: What do you think this rhythm strip shows?
e: Regular rate about 100-120 with a P before each QRS: sinus tachycardia.

questions.q: This ECG shows:
e: Regular narrow tachycardia with P waves, normal PR: sinus tachycardia.

questions.q: What is the correct diagnosis?
e: Very fast regular narrow-complex tachycardia: SVT.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
e: Very fast regular narrow-complex tachycardia: SVT.

questions.q: Select the right answer:
e: Regular saw-tooth atrial activity: atrial flutter.

questions.q: Select the right answer:
e: Flutter waves with variable QRS response: atrial flutter.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: Regular wide-complex rapid rhythm: VT.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
e: Uniform wide QRS complexes: monomorphic VT.

questions.q: What is your diagnosis for the beat at the tip of the arrow?
e: Early wide bizarre beat (arrow) with no preceding P: PVC.

questions.q: Select the correct answer:
e: Short PR and delta wave: WPW (accessory pathway).

questions.q: A 25-year-old asymptomatic tennis player. His rhythm strip is shown. What is this rhythm?
e: Regular rate about 50/min with normal P-QRS in an athlete: sinus bradycardia.

questions.q: A 25-year-old asymptomatic tennis player. His rhythm strip is shown. This patient needs a pacemaker.
e: Sinus bradycardia in an asymptomatic athlete is physiological; no pacemaker needed.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
e: Long PR interval (>200 ms) with every P conducted: first-degree block.

questions.q: Select the proper answer:
o: Second degree heart block type I
e: Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat: Mobitz I (Wenckebach).

questions.q: The following ECG reveals:
o: Mobitz type 2 second degree heart block
e: Progressive PR prolongation until a non-conducted P: Wenckebach.

questions.q: This ECG shows evidence of:
o: Second degree Mobitz type 1 heart block
Second degree Mobitz type 2 heart block
e: Progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beat: Mobitz I.

questions.q: This ECG shows evidence of:
o: Second degree Mobitz type 1 heart block
Second degree Mobitz type 2 heart block
e: Constant PR with sudden non-conducted P waves: Mobitz II.

questions.q: What is your diagnosis?
e: Non-conducted P waves: second-degree heart block.

questions.q: A 73-year-old female with recurrent attacks of fainting. Her rhythm strip shows:
e: Three P waves per QRS: 3:1 block.

questions.q: An 80-year-old female patient presents with recurrent attacks of syncope. Her ECG shows: What is your diagnosis?
e: Dissociated P waves and slow regular QRS: complete heart block.

questions.q: The heart rate in this ECG (lead II) is:
e: R-R about 4.3 large squares: about 70/min.

questions.q: In second degree Mobitz type 2 heart block, which of the following ECG abnormalities is typically seen?
o: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval until an atrial impulse is completely blocked and does not produce a QRS complex.
Progressive shortening of the PR interval until an atrial impulse is completely blocked and does not produce a QRS complex.
Intermittently non-conducted P waves not preceded by PR prolongation.
e: Mobitz II: intermittent non-conducted P without preceding PR lengthening.

questions.q: In second degree heart block, Mobitz type 1, which of the following statements is correct?
o: There is gradually progressive PR interval prolongation before the blocked sinus impulse.
There is fixed prolongation of the PR interval.
There is progressive widening of the QRS complexes.
e: Mobitz I: progressive PR prolongation before the blocked impulse.

questions.q: All of the following are considered modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease EXCEPT:
e: Age is a non-modifiable risk factor.

questions.q: A 58 year old patient complains of retrosternal chest pain of few minutes duration, precipitated by walking briskly and relieved by rest. His pulse is 92/min regular, BP 130/80. The chest and cardiac examination were normal. The patient will benefit from the following medications to relieve his symptoms and improve his condition, EXCEPT:
e: Angina treatment: beta-blockers, aspirin, nitrates; loop diuretics give no anti-ischaemic benefit.

questions.q: Anti-ischemic measures for patients with stable chronic angina may include the following EXCEPT:
e: Tirofiban (GP IIb/IIIa) is for ACS/PCI, not stable angina.

questions.q: A 63-year-old man presents with episodic retrosternal chest tightness after physical exertion lasting for few minutes and is relieved by rest. The condition has a stationary course over 6 months. The resting ECG is normal and he has no history of hypertension or diabetes. Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosing this condition?
e: Typical stable angina with a normal resting ECG: exercise ECG next.

questions.q: Acute coronary syndromes include the following EXCEPT:
e: ACS comprises STEMI, NSTEMI and unstable angina; variant angina is vasospastic.

questions.q: The key to differentiating NSTEMI from unstable angina is:
e: Troponin/enzyme rise separates NSTEMI from unstable angina.

questions.q: All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: Typical chest pain could radiate to the jaw
Epigastric pain (without the chest component of the pain) could be the only symptom in some patients with ACS
Normal troponin levels exclude typical chest pain
Invasive coronary angiography is indicated in patients with high-risk non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome
e: A normal troponin does not exclude typical angina (stable or unstable angina has normal troponin).

questions.q: One year ago, a 63-year-old man started to complain of episodic retrosternal chest tightness after moderate physical exertion, lasting for few minutes and relieved by rest. The patient presents to the ER complaining of the same chest pain at rest. He describes that in the last 3 weeks the same pain was precipitated by minimal effort, lasts longer than before and is relieved by sublingual nitrates. The resting ECG shows dynamic 2 mm horizontal ST segment depression in anterior leads. Cardiac enzymes were repeatedly normal. What is the most likely diagnosis of this condition?
o: Non ST segment elevation myocardial infarction
e: Crescendo pattern, dynamic ST depression, normal enzymes = unstable angina.

questions.q: A 47-year-old male patient presented to the ER with prolonged chest pain without elevation of the cardiac enzymes. This ECG was done during chest pain. What should be done?
o: Transfer him to the cath lab as STEMI
Admit him to CCU as a case of unstable angina
Admit him to CCU as a case of NSTEMI
e: Chest pain with ST/T changes and negative enzymes: unstable angina, admit to CCU.

questions.q: In non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction:
o: The patient may present with crescendo angina
The ECG may show significant horizontal ST segment depression
e: NSTEMI: crescendo angina, ST depression and raised enzymes. All true.

questions.q: A 67-year-old man presents to A&E with central chest pain radiating up to his jaw. He describes it as a 'heaviness' and feels sweaty. It started an hour ago and has got progressively worse. He has never had a pain like this before. He has a past medical history of hypertension and takes amlodipine for it. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has a 70 pack-year history. His ECG shows significant ST depression in leads II, III and aVF. Lab results show elevated troponin level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Ischaemic symptoms, ST depression and raised troponin = NSTEMI.

questions.q: A 63 year old man presents to the ER complaining of severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to both shoulders of 2 hours duration, associated with excessive sweating. The pulse was 110/min with a pulse volume equal on both arms and normal peripheral pulsations. The BP was 120/80 equal on both arms. Blood gases revealed normal PO2 and normal PCO2. Cardiac examination revealed normal heart sounds with a fourth heart sound over the apex. Chest examination was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Severe retrosternal pain with sweating and an S4 (ventricular dysfunction) fits ACS. Equal pulses and blood pressure in both arms argue against aortic dissection, normal blood gases against pulmonary embolism, and a normal chest examination against tension pneumothorax.

questions.q: A male patient presenting to the ER with severe retrosternal chest pain, who is vitally stable; the most important next step is:
o: Send him to the cath lab
Take blood samples for cardiac enzymes
e: First step in chest pain is a 12-lead ECG.

questions.q: A 75-year-old man presents to the ER with a 3-hour history of intense retrosternal chest pain. He is known to be hypertensive for 20 years and diabetic for 5 years. He does not smoke. The BP is 180/110 in both arms, the HR is 84/min and RR is 18/min. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
e: Equal BP in both arms; ECG first to identify STEMI.

questions.q: A 54 year old man presents with central crushing chest pain. Examination is normal. 12-lead ECG shows ST segment elevation in leads V1 to V3 and ST depression in leads II and III. The most possible diagnosis is:
o: Acute anteroseptal ST elevation myocardial infarction
Acute ST elevation inferior myocardial infarction
e: ST elevation V1-V3 with reciprocal depression II, III: anteroseptal STEMI.

questions.q: A 54 year old man presents with central crushing chest pain. Examination is normal. 12-lead ECG shows ST segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF and marked ST depression in V1-V3. The most possible diagnosis is:
o: Acute anteroseptal ST elevation myocardial infarction
Acute ST elevation inferoposterior myocardial infarction
e: ST elevation II, III, aVF with ST depression V1-V3: inferoposterior STEMI.

questions.q: Select the correct diagnosis:
e: ST elevation V1-V4: anterior STEMI.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
o: Recent extensive anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction
e: Extensive ST elevation across anterior and lateral leads: anterolateral STEMI.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
e: Extensive anterior ST elevation.

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis:
e: ST elevation II, III, aVF: inferior STEMI.

questions.q: Select the correct answer:
e: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes: acute inferior MI.

questions.q: A patient presents to the ER with severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left shoulder, of 1 hour duration and associated with excessive sweating. The ECG done in the ER is shown below. This ECG is consistent with a diagnosis of:
e: ST elevation in V1-V4: acute anterior STEMI.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male patient, smoker, hypertensive, with severe central chest pain radiating to his shoulders, associated with nausea; he is vitally stable. His ECG shows:
e: ST elevation in anterior leads: anterior STEMI.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents to the ER with central chest pain for 5 hours. This ECG is done within 10 min from reaching the hospital. This patient is having:
e: ST elevation in anterior leads: anterior STEMI.

questions.q: Select the best next step in this patient who presents with severe retrosternal chest pain of 2 hours duration (ECG shown):
e: STEMI: aspirin loading, a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or clopidogrel), and primary PCI are all indicated.

questions.q: Select the best next step in this patient who presents with severe retrosternal chest pain of 2 hours duration (ECG shown):
o: Fibrinolytic therapy if primary PCI is not available
f: Conflicting keys: bank key D (all of the above), Dr. Hawary key B (primary PCI).
e: All three are correct components of STEMI care: dual antiplatelet therapy, primary PCI as the preferred reperfusion strategy, and fibrinolysis when timely primary PCI is unavailable.

questions.q: A patient presents to the ER with severe retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left shoulder, of 1 hour duration and associated with excessive sweating. The ECG done in the ER is shown below. The best management of this patient would be:
o: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to open the occluded coronary vessel
Thrombolytic therapy if primary PCI is not available
Dual antiplatelet therapy in the form of aspirin and clopidogrel
e: STEMI: primary PCI to open the occluded vessel, thrombolysis if primary PCI is unavailable, and dual antiplatelet therapy are all correct components.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents to the ER with central chest pain for 5 hours. The ECG is done within 10 min from reaching the hospital. What is the next step after your diagnosis?
o: Refer to cath lab for PCI
e: Anterior STEMI: refer to cath lab for primary PCI.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male patient, smoker, hypertensive, with severe central chest pain radiating to his shoulders, associated with nausea; he is vitally stable. His ECG shows anterior STEMI (ECG shown). The most appropriate next step in this patient should be:
o: Send the patient to the cath lab
Refer the patient to the chest pain unit and wait for cardiac enzymes result
Call the cardiology resident to reassess the situation
e: STEMI: send to the cath lab immediately.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male patient, smoker, hypertensive, with severe central chest pain radiating to his shoulders, associated with nausea; he is vitally stable. His ECG shows anterior STEMI (ECG shown). While you transfer the patient, what should you do?
o: Put the patient empirically on oxygen
Give aspirin 300 mg with clopidogrel or ticagrelor
e: During transfer: aspirin loading plus a P2Y12 inhibitor; oxygen only if hypoxic.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presented to the ER at midnight in a large tertiary hospital with a 2-hour history of central chest tightness radiating to his jaw. He is sweaty and nauseous. The pain has not responded to repeated doses of his own nitrates. On examination he is pale and clammy, HR 110 bpm, BP 100/60. Otherwise his examination is grossly normal. ECG shows ST elevation across leads V1-V5, with reciprocal ST depression in lead III. What is the gold standard therapy for this man's problem?
o: Urgent thrombolytic therapy then coronary angiography the next day
Immediate subcutaneous enoxaparin then coronary angiography after stabilization
e: STEMI in a PCI-capable tertiary centre: primary PCI is the gold standard.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents to the ER in a large tertiary hospital with a 2-hour history of central chest tightness radiating down his left arm. He is sweaty and nauseous. The pain has not responded to repeated doses of his own GTN. On examination he is pale and clammy, HR 110 bpm, BP 107/59. Otherwise his examination is grossly normal. ECG shows ST elevation across leads V1-V5, with reciprocal ST depression in lead III. Trop T is elevated at 45. What is the gold standard therapy for this man's problem?
e: STEMI in a PCI centre: primary PCI.

questions.q: A 59-year-old male known to be diabetic presents to the emergency room with severe chest pain of 1 hour duration. His BP is 160/106. The echo shows an EF of 45%. The ECG shows: What is the recommended first line of treatment?
e: STEMI: primary PCI first line.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents at midnight to a non-PCI-capable hospital with 2 hours of central chest pain radiating to the jaw, unrelieved by nitrates. Diaphoretic. HR 100, BP 130/70. ECG: ST-segment elevation in V1-V5 with ST- segment depression in lead III. The nearest primary PCI-capable centre is 30 minutes away. The optimal management is:
o: Administer fibrinolysis immediately, then arrange angiography after 12 hours
Fibrinolysis followed by risk stratification and selective referral
e: PCI centre 30 minutes away (well under 120 min): transfer for primary PCI.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents to a rural community clinic with 1 hour of crushing chest pain. Her ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1-V4. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is 3 hours away by ambulance. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Wait for transfer to the PCI center because primary PCI is always superior to thrombolysis
Administer thrombolytic therapy immediately and arrange for transfer to a PCI-capable center
Give aspirin and morphine only, and monitor until symptoms resolve
Start heparin infusion and schedule elective coronary angiography next week
e: PCI 3 hours away (>120 min): fibrinolysis immediately then transfer.

questions.q: In the ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) setting, all of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
o: In the setting of STEMI, a loading dose of aspirin and one of the P2Y12 receptor inhibitors is recommended
Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (pPCI) is recommended over fibrinolysis if the anticipated time from diagnosis to PCI is <120 min
If timely pPCI (<120 min) cannot be performed in patients with STEMI, fibrinolytic therapy is recommended
Clopidogrel for a duration of up to 3 months following STEMI is the standard of care
e: Clopidogrel/DAPT is continued up to 12 months after STEMI, not 3 months.

questions.q: All of the following are contraindications to thrombolytic therapy for STEMI EXCEPT:
o: All of the above are contraindications to thrombolytic therapy
e: All three are absolute contraindications to thrombolysis: recent hemorrhagic stroke and active bleeding match the book's list (stroke within 1 year, bleeding tendency), and intracranial neoplasm carries the same intracranial bleeding risk.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male recovering from anterior MI develops sudden onset of severe left side chest pain. He appears agitated. Two minutes later he is unresponsive. His pulse is not palpable and ECG monitoring shows sinus tachycardia at a rate of 130/min. He is known to be a smoker, diabetic and overweight. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Pulseless electrical activity with sinus rhythm after MI: free wall rupture.

questions.q: The main complications of a left ventricular aneurysm include the following EXCEPT:
e: VT, heart failure and LV thrombus are LV aneurysm complications; SVT is not a main one.

questions.q: A 67-year-old man presents to A&E with central chest pain radiating up to his jaw. He describes it as a 'heaviness' and feels sweaty. It started an hour ago and has got progressively worse. He has never had a pain like this before. He has a past medical history of hypertension and takes amlodipine for it. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has a 70 pack-year history. His ECG shows significant ST depression in leads II, III and aVF. Select the next step in this patient:
f: Ambiguous: NSTEMI next step could also include a P2Y12 inhibitor.
e: In NSTEMI, aspirin is the immediate first step; a P2Y12 inhibitor follows as part of dual antiplatelet therapy, while immediate primary PCI is STEMI management and is not routine in NSTEMI.

questions.q: The complications of myocardial infarction include the following EXCEPT:
f: Atrial arrhythmias can also complicate MI; keyed answer kept.
e: The book lists ventricular arrhythmias, heart failure, and ventricular aneurysm among the complications of MI; supraventricular tachycardia is not among the main listed complications.

questions.q: A 53-year-old female presents to the physician's office with a 3-week history of retrosternal burning chest pain, usually on exertion and relieved by rest. The pain does not radiate to the arm or jaw. Stable angina is suspected and the patient is scheduled for an exercise ECG test. Which of the following medications should be withheld 24 hours before the test?
e: Beta-blockers blunt heart rate response, so they are withheld before an exercise ECG. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: Select the proper diagnosis of this ECG:
e: Q waves with persistent ST elevation in anterior leads: old anterior MI.

questions.q: 63-year-old man presents to the emergency room complaining of severe compressing retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm of 2 hours duration. The examination revealed a pulse of 120/min and BP was measured 110/80. The cardiac examination revealed an S4 over the apex. The chest examination revealed bilateral fine basal crepitations. What would you order first to diagnose the patient?
e: ECG first for acute chest pain.

questions.q: Select the correct answer.
e: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes: inferior MI.

questions.q: Systemic hypertension is diagnosed if the blood pressure is:
e: Hypertension: >=140/90 mmHg.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man is referred from the general practitioner for management of uncontrolled hypertension associated with headache. The BP is 180/110 and HR is 86 bpm. Cardiac examination reveals accentuated A2 and S4. Chest auscultation shows normal sounds with no basal crepitation. The ECG shows LVH. Which of the following is the least likely to be a cause of hypertension in this patient?
o: CRF due to intrinsic renal disease
e: Young patient with severe hypertension: secondary causes more likely than essential.

questions.q: When to suspect secondary hypertension?
o: Onset of hypertension before age 25 or after age 60 years
Poor response to prior effective drug therapy
Paroxysmal attacks of hypertension with palpitation, pallor, sweating and tremors
e: Early or late onset, resistant hypertension, loss of response to previously effective therapy, and paroxysmal pheochromocytoma-like attacks all suggest a secondary cause (book: onset <30 or >50 years).

questions.q: Essential uncomplicated hypertension usually presents by:
e: Uncomplicated essential hypertension is usually asymptomatic.

questions.q: Routine investigations of hypertensive patients should include all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Urine protein electrophoresis is not routine.

questions.q: A 43-year-old male presents to your clinic with systemic hypertension. He is a non-smoker and not known to be diabetic. He has a normal creatinine and potassium. His BP cannot reach the target by lifestyle modification or monotherapy with an ACE inhibitor. The BP becomes well controlled by a combination of an ACE inhibitor and a calcium channel blocker. What is the target BP in this patient?
e: Current guidelines target below 130/80 or so, so none of the listed values.

questions.q: A 57-year-old male patient who is known to have diabetic nephropathy with macro-albuminuria. The target of lowering his BP is:
e: Diabetic nephropathy with albuminuria: target below 130/80.

questions.q: Non-pharmacological lines of therapy in hypertensive patients include all EXCEPT:
o: Increase fruit and vegetables in diet
e: Weight reduction is itself a non-pharmacological therapy, but the book's target is BMI <25 kg/m² — the option's BMI <30 wording is what makes it the exception.

questions.q: A 43-year-old woman with diabetes for 10 years and hypertension for 5 years is seen in the OPD for follow-up. Her current medication is metformin 500 mg tds, gliclazide 80 mg od, simvastatin 40 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg od, telmisartan (ARB) 80 mg od and amlodipine 5 mg od. Her BP is 150/90 and the medical officer decides to add metoprolol 50 mg bd. Which of the following statements is correct?
o: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the preferred starting medications in diabetics
Thiazides are the preferred starting medications in diabetics
Beta blockers are the preferred starting medications in diabetics
Centrally acting drugs are the preferred starting medications in diabetics
e: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred in diabetes: RAS blockade reduces albuminuria and slows nephropathy in addition to lowering BP.

questions.q: In a pregnant female, which drug can be used safely?
e: Methyldopa is safe in pregnancy; ACE inhibitors are contraindicated.

questions.q: All of the following can be used in treating a hypertensive patient EXCEPT:
e: Peripheral alpha-adrenergic stimulation raises blood pressure and is not an antihypertensive mechanism; usable classes include beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and centrally acting drugs (central α2 agonists).

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding management of hypertensive emergencies?
o: Rapidly acting sublingual nifedipine and captopril are the drugs of choice
Intravenous diuretics can be used as good alternatives
In hypertensive urgencies, BP is lowered gradually over a period of 24 to 48 hours with oral medication
The immediate goal of IV therapy is to reduce the DBP by 25% or to about 110 mmHg in 15 minutes
e: In hypertensive urgency (no target-organ damage) there is no benefit from rapid reduction: lower BP gradually to ≤160/100 over hours to days with oral drugs, and avoid sublingual nifedipine/captopril, whose fall in BP is uncontrolled.

questions.q: Hypertensive urgency differs from hypertensive emergency regarding:
o: Both present with target organ damage
Both have to be managed immediately with IV drugs
Both can be managed immediately with oral medications
Hypertensive emergency presents with target organ damage while hypertensive urgency does not
e: Emergency has acute target-organ damage; urgency does not.

questions.q: In management of resistant hypertension, we should consider all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Drug interactions / excessive sodium intake / alcohol
e: Liver failure does not cause resistant hypertension.

questions.q: The cut-off value for diagnosing hypertension in ambulatory and home readings is:
e: As keyed: 130/80 for ambulatory/home (guideline-dependent, ESC uses 135/85). Flagged. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: ACE inhibitors are among the commonest and most useful drugs in hypertension and cardiovascular disease, but are contraindicated in a few conditions. In which of the following are ACE inhibitors absolutely contraindicated? (more than one answer)
e: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy and angioedema, and in bilateral renal artery stenosis. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: In a patient with isolated left-sided heart failure, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
o: The patient may complain of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
The chest examination may reveal bilateral fine basal rales
The heart examination may reveal a third heart sound over the cardiac apex
The heart examination may reveal a third heart sound over the tricuspid area
e: In left HF, S3 is at the apex; tricuspid-area S3 is right-sided.

questions.q: In a patient with isolated left-sided heart failure, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
o: The patient may complain of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
The chest examination may reveal bilateral fine basal rales
The liver may be enlarged and pulsating
The heart examination may reveal a third heart sound over the cardiac apex
e: Pulsating enlarged liver suggests right-sided failure/TR.

questions.q: Symptoms and signs of isolated left-sided heart failure include all the following EXCEPT:
o: Third heart sound gallop over the apex
e: Right hypochondrial pain is right HF (hepatic congestion).

questions.q: In a patient with isolated right-sided heart failure, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
o: The patient may complain of bilateral lower limb edema
The chest examination may reveal bilateral fine basal rales
The heart examination may reveal a third heart sound over the tricuspid area
The heart examination may reveal a pansystolic murmur over the tricuspid area that increases with inspiration
e: Basal rales occur in left HF, not isolated right HF.

questions.q: A patient with symptoms and signs of left-sided heart failure is subjected to echocardiography which revealed an ejection fraction of 35%. This confirms the diagnosis of:
o: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
e: EF <40%: HFrEF.

questions.q: A patient with symptoms and signs of left-sided heart failure is subjected to echocardiography which revealed an ejection fraction of 46%. This confirms the diagnosis of:
o: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
e: EF 40–49%: heart failure with mid-range EF.

questions.q: A patient with symptoms and signs of left-sided heart failure is subjected to echocardiography which revealed an ejection fraction of 55%. This confirms the diagnosis of:
o: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
e: EF >=50%: HFpEF.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man has a nine-month history of worsening breathlessness. His blood pressure is 160/95 mmHg, O2 saturation 90% on air, temperature 36.5°C; there is an apical S4 and bilateral basal lung crepitations. He has high cholesterol and triglycerides. The ECG shows LVH and the echo shows concentric hypertrophy and EF is 60%. How can you classify this case according to the EF?
e: EF 60% with hypertrophy: HFpEF.

questions.q: Signs of heart failure include the following EXCEPT:
o: Bilateral basal crepitations on chest auscultation
e: In HF the JVP is raised and pulsatile (prominent v waves if tricuspid regurgitation); congested non-pulsating neck veins are the book's description of tamponade, not HF.

questions.q: The following is suggestive of heart failure EXCEPT:
e: Central cyanosis is not a sign of heart failure.

questions.q: A patient comes to the ER with acute shortness of breath and a cough producing pink, frothy sputum. Admission assessment reveals crackles and wheezes, BP 95/50, HR 122/min and respiratory rate 38/min. The medical history includes DM, hypertension and heart failure. Which of the following disorders should you suspect?
e: Pink frothy sputum with crackles, tachypnea and hypoxia in a patient with known HF is acute pulmonary edema — severe left HF with alveolar flooding.

questions.q: All of the following drugs can be used in the treatment of heart failure EXCEPT:
e: Calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, nifedipine) may depress LV function and are best avoided in heart failure.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man has left ventricular failure and clinically he is classified as NYHA class III. He takes furosemide, aspirin and ramipril. The addition of which one of the following would be expected to further improve his prognosis?
e: Beta-blocker (bisoprolol) improves prognosis in HFrEF.

questions.q: A 58-year-old patient complains of shortness of breath at rest, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. His pulse is 120/min, irregularly irregular (AF). BP 130/80. Chest examination reveals bilateral basal fine crepitations and cardiac examination reveals a third heart sound gallop over the apex. The patient will benefit from all the following medications to relieve his symptoms and improve his condition EXCEPT:
o: Oral beta blockers starting with the maximum possible dose
e: Beta-blockers are started low in decompensated patients, not at maximum dose.

questions.q: A 43-year-old female presents to your clinic complaining of dyspnea and palpitations. The BP is 130/80. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia and LVH. Chest X-ray reveals increased CT ratio with Kerley B lines. Echocardiography shows dilated LV with EF = 35% and moderate mitral regurgitation. Which of the following treatments is NOT recommended?
e: ARBs are antagonists; "receptor stimulants" are wrong.

questions.q: A 53-year-old male is admitted to the hospital with a 2-week history of fatigue, dyspnea and decrease in effort tolerance. His BP is 150/90 and HR is 130/min. Lungs are clear on auscultation. Echocardiography shows dilated LV with EF of 35% and moderate mitral regurgitation. A rhythm strip of lead II is shown. All of the following lines are recommended EXCEPT:
e: Calcium antagonists may depress LV function and are best avoided in HF; ACE inhibitors, anticoagulation (AF) and digitalis are recommended.

questions.q: In a patient with isolated left-sided systolic heart failure, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
o: The patient may complain of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
The chest examination may reveal bilateral fine basal rales
The heart examination may reveal a third heart sound over the cardiac apex
The heart examination may reveal a fourth heart sound over the apex
e: S4 comes from atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle; in systolic HF the LV is dilated and compliant, so the gallop is S3, not S4. (Exam-keyed.)

questions.q: A 15-year-old female is found to have a heart murmur during routine examination. She had a febrile illness with fleeting joint swelling and pain one year ago. She plays table tennis and swims every weekend. On cardiac examination there is a loud first heart sound and a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. Lungs are clear to auscultation. The BP is 110/70 and HR is 80/min regular. ECG is normal. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient at this point?
e: Post-rheumatic MS with established rheumatic heart disease: secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units IM every 4 weeks, continued indefinitely. It prevents streptococcal recurrence and further valve damage; beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors and anticoagulation have no such role here.

questions.q: Regarding the pathology of rheumatic mitral stenosis:
o: Large friable vegetations are seen on the mitral valve leaflets.
Fibrosis of the leaflets occurs with fusion of the commissures.
An area of 1.5 cm2 is considered severe (tight) mitral stenosis.
Mitral valve leaflets are redundant and myxomatous.
e: Rheumatic MS: leaflet fibrosis and commissural fusion.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male admitted with dyspnea. The BP is 110/80 and HR is 88/min. Auscultation reveals a murmur suggestive of mitral stenosis. The presence of which of the following clinical signs suggests that the mitral valve is pliable?
e: Opening snap indicates a pliable valve.

questions.q: A 79-year-old woman has had worsening shortness of breath for several years. She now has to sleep sitting up on two pillows. She has difficulty swallowing. Recently, she suffered a stroke with left hemiparesis. A chest X-ray reveals a near normal left ventricular size with a prominent left atrial border. Which of the following conditions is most likely to account for these findings?
e: Mitral stenosis: a giant left atrium compresses the oesophagus (dysphagia) and predisposes to atrial fibrillation with systemic embolism (stroke); a near-normal left ventricle with a prominent left atrial border fits MS, not cardiomyopathy or hypertension.

questions.q: A 27-year-old female with history of rheumatic heart disease presents with palpitation and dyspnea that increased acutely and markedly over the previous few hours. She is coughing frothy blood-tinged sputum. Her blood pressure is 80/48, heart rate 130 beats/min and irregular, respiratory rate 38 cycles/min, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. Physical examination revealed bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations and elevated jugular venous pressure. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rumbling diastolic murmur over the apex. Which of the following is the most possible cause of her acute symptoms?
e: Acute pulmonary oedema in MS from new AF (rapid rate shortens diastole).

questions.q: All the following statements about severe mitral stenosis and atrial fibrillation are correct EXCEPT:
o: The patient should receive oral anticoagulation for life.
A loud first heart sound is heard over the apex.
A mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with presystolic accentuation is heard over the apex.
A narrow time interval between the second heart sound and opening snap is heard.
e: Presystolic accentuation is absent in AF (no atrial contraction).

questions.q: Patients with mitral stenosis and atrial fibrillation:
o: Should receive oral anticoagulation for life.
Should receive oral anticoagulation only if they develop thromboembolic complications.
Should receive aspirin only if they develop thromboembolic complications.
e: MS with AF: lifelong oral anticoagulation.

questions.q: Elderly patients with aortic stenosis and atrial fibrillation:
o: Should receive oral anticoagulation for life.
Should receive oral anticoagulation only if they develop thromboembolic complications.
Should receive aspirin only if they develop thromboembolic complications.
e: Elderly patients with AF: age ≥75 alone scores 2 on CHA2DS2-VASc, so long-term oral anticoagulation is indicated; aspirin is not a substitute. (Aortic stenosis itself is not the indication — the stroke-risk score is.)

questions.q: A 33-year-old female presents to the ER with recent left-sided hemiplegia. She is known to have paroxysmal arrhythmia over the last year on top of rheumatic heart disease. The BP is 110/80 and HR is 100 bpm. Cardiac examination reveals accentuated S1, an apical mid-diastolic rumbling murmur and accentuated P2. The echocardiography is illustrated below. The patient is non-compliant to the treatment. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the cerebrovascular stroke if discontinued?
e: Stroke from rheumatic MS/AF prevented by warfarin; non-compliance explains the event.

questions.q: A distressed patient is brought to the ER by ambulance. He is short of breath with a respiratory rate of 34 cycles/min and BP 120/82 mmHg. He has a rumbling diastolic murmur over the heart with presystolic accentuation. He has bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations over the lungs. The first step in treatment is to:
e: Acute pulmonary oedema in MS (crepitations, tachypnoea): relieve congestion first with IV diuretics (frusemide). DC cardioversion has no role — presystolic accentuation means sinus rhythm is present and the patient is normotensive.

questions.q: A 23-year-old female presents to your clinic with shortness of breath on ordinary effort over the last year. The BP is 90/60 mmHg, the HR is 100/min and the JVP is normal. Examination revealed an apical mid-diastolic rumbling murmur and accentuated P2. The ECG shows P-mitrale and sinus tachycardia. The echocardiography shows tight mitral stenosis with MVA = 0.9 cm2. In severe mitral stenosis, balloon mitral valvuloplasty is preferred over mitral valve replacement in which of the following situations?
o: Pliable valve with minimal affection of subvalvular apparatus
e: Balloon valvuloplasty suits a pliable valve with minimal subvalvular disease.

questions.q: Balloon mitral valvotomy can be done in all cases EXCEPT:
o: A pliable (non-calcific) stenotic mitral valve with pulmonary hypertension.
A stenotic mitral valve with severe calcification.
A pliable stenotic mitral valve with tricuspid regurge.
A pliable severely stenotic mitral valve.
e: Severe calcification contraindicates balloon valvotomy.

questions.q: Balloon mitral valvotomy is preferred to surgery in:
o: Apex localized in the 6th intercostal space
Opening snap heard at the apex
e: Opening snap = pliable valve.

questions.q: Which of the following is a functional cause of mitral regurgitation?
e: Dilated cardiomyopathy dilates the left ventricle and mitral annulus, so structurally normal leaflets fail to coapt — functional MR. Prolapse, endocarditis and rheumatic disease damage the valve itself (organic MR).

questions.q: Mitral regurgitation can be caused by:
e: All listed cause MR.

questions.q: A 29-year-old female patient who is on long-acting penicillin presents to the clinic with palpitation. On examination there is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla with muffled S1. The valvular lesion is:
e: Pansystolic apical murmur to the axilla: MR.

questions.q: History: 50-year-old male with dyspnea FC IV, orthopnea and PND. General examination: pulse 100 bpm, irregular, normal volume; BP 120/80 mmHg; raised JVP with systolic 'v' waves and peripheral edema. Cardiac inspection and palpation: apex shifted downwards and outwards with thrusting quality; parasternal heave and parasternal thrill. Cardiac auscultation: soft S1 and accentuated P2, S3 over the apex; pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla (best in expiration in the left lateral position); pansystolic murmur at the LLSB increasing with inspiration (TR). Chest auscultation: bibasal crepitations. What is the most probable diagnosis?
e: Chronic severe MR: pansystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla, soft S1, S3 and a displaced thrusting apex from left ventricular volume overload. The inspiratory pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with systolic v waves is functional tricuspid regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension.

questions.q: Which of the following is FALSE regarding the pathophysiology of mitral regurgitation?
o: Cardiac hemodynamics are the same for acute and chronic MR.
LA pressure is normal or mildly elevated with no marked changes in the forward CO in chronic compensated MR.
LA pressure is markedly elevated and CO is decreased in acute MR.
LA pressure is elevated and CO is decreased in chronic decompensated MR.
e: Acute and chronic MR have different haemodynamics.

questions.q: Which of the following may be a presenting symptom of mitral regurgitation?
o: Left or right sided heart failure manifestations
e: MR can present with all listed.

questions.q: All of the following are clinical markers for mitral regurgitation severity EXCEPT:
e: Murmur loudness does not reflect MR severity.

questions.q: The following statements regarding ACUTE severe mitral regurgitation are all correct EXCEPT:
o: The patient may present with acute pulmonary edema.
The left atrium is markedly enlarged.
Requires urgent surgical repair or replacement of the mitral valve.
e: In acute MR the left atrium is NOT enlarged.

questions.q: All of the following is true regarding medical management in patients with severe mitral regurgitation EXCEPT:
o: Vasodilators and loop diuretics (as furosemide or torsemide) are beneficial and so indicated in asymptomatic patients.
Vasodilators and loop diuretics are indicated only in symptomatic patients not candidate for surgery or if severely symptomatic as a bridge to surgery.
Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis and long acting penicillin are required.
Oral anticoagulation if AF or previous embolization.
e: Vasodilators are not recommended in asymptomatic MR.

questions.q: A 22-year-old girl presents with palpitation and non-exertional infra-mammary chest pain over the past few weeks. On presentation she was anxious. Physical examination reveals a heart rate of 99 bpm, blood pressure of 98/60 mmHg, normal JVP, a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
o: Congenital aortic stenosis due to bicuspid aortic valve
e: Mid-systolic click with late systolic murmur: MVP.

questions.q: Major etiologies of aortic valve stenosis include all EXCEPT:
e: Marfan does not cause AS.

questions.q: The commonest cause of congenital aortic stenosis is:
e: Bicuspid valve is the commonest congenital AS cause.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding severe aortic stenosis are correct EXCEPT:
o: The mortality is significantly increased once symptoms start; particularly the heart failure symptoms
Syncope is one of the symptoms in patients with severe aortic stenosis
Bicuspid aortic valve is a very rare cause of aortic stenosis
Degenerative calcific aortic valve disease is a common aetiology in elderly
e: Bicuspid aortic valve is a common cause, not rare.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the clinical findings in a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
o: Ejection systolic murmur which increases with inspiration.
Ejection systolic murmur with delayed peaking.
Muffled pulmonary component of the second heart sound.
Ejection systolic murmur with early peaking.
e: AS murmur is late-peaking.

questions.q: A 73-year-old male presents to the ER because he lost consciousness while working in the garden. He has had several episodes of near-syncope on exertion recently. He is not taking any medication. Cardiac examination reveals an ejection systolic murmur at the base of the heart with radiation to the carotid arteries, consistent with severe calcific aortic stenosis. What is the most probable cause of his syncope?
e: Exertional syncope in severe AS: the fixed stenotic valve prevents cardiac output from rising with exercise, so cerebral perfusion falls when peripheral vasodilatation occurs. The book lists aortic stenosis among the obstructive causes of syncope.

questions.q: The main line of treatment of symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is:
e: Surgical AVR for symptomatic severe AS.

questions.q: A distressed patient is brought to the ER by ambulance. He is short of breath with a respiratory rate of 34 cycles/min, BP 120/40 mmHg and his heart rate is 110/min. He has a long-standing early diastolic decrescendo murmur over the second aortic area. He has bilateral fine inspiratory crepitations over the lungs. The first step in treatment is to:
e: Wide pulse pressure (120/40) with an early diastolic decrescendo murmur = aortic regurgitation; acute pulmonary oedema (crepitations, tachypnoea) is treated first with IV diuretics (frusemide).

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding tricuspid valve diseases are correct EXCEPT:
o: The intensity of tricuspid regurgitation murmur increases during inspiration and leg raising
Cachexia and jaundice could be associated with long-standing severe tricuspid regurgitation.
In severe tricuspid regurgitation, jugular venous pressure is usually high with a systolic collapse
Carcinoid syndrome may cause tricuspid valve disease
e: In TR the JVP shows systolic EXPANSION, not collapse.

questions.q: Which of the following can lead to functional tricuspid regurgitation?
e: Severe mitral stenosis raises pulmonary pressures, dilating the right ventricle and tricuspid annulus — functional tricuspid regurgitation with a structurally normal valve. Endocarditis and rheumatic tricuspid disease damage the valve itself (organic disease), and Fallot tetralogy does not cause functional TR.

questions.q: The most common cause of mitral stenosis is:
e: Rheumatic heart disease is the commonest cause of MS.

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding mitral stenosis?
o: It is tolerated well during atrial fibrillation
There is characteristically a low pulmonary wedge pressure
In AF, the opening snap disappears
The opening snap is not heard when the mitral valve is heavily calcified
e: Opening snap lost in heavily calcified MS.

questions.q: In mitral stenosis, a narrow time interval between the second heart sound and the opening snap indicates:
e: Narrow S2-OS interval = severe MS.

questions.q: Which of the following is a sign of severe mitral stenosis?
o: An opening snap close to the first heart sound
An opening snap close to the second heart sound
An ejection click close to the second heart sound
e: OS close to S2 signals severe MS.

questions.q: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with acute onset of left-sided weakness. She has a history of progressive dyspnea, nocturnal cough and occasional hemoptysis over the past year. She also describes frequent episodes of irregular palpitation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Mitral stenosis: pulmonary congestion causes progressive dyspnoea, nocturnal cough and haemoptysis; left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation (irregular palpitation) and systemic embolism (stroke with left-sided weakness).

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with previous rheumatic heart disease has been lost to follow-up for some time. She now has symptoms of breathlessness. On examination, she has an apical diastolic murmur and a large V wave in the JVP. What is the likely diagnosis?
e: Diastolic apical murmur plus large v wave: MS with TR.

questions.q: All the following are typical complications of long-standing isolated mitral stenosis EXCEPT:
e: In isolated mitral stenosis the left ventricle is underfilled and small, not dilated — the pressure load falls on the left atrium and the pulmonary circulation, causing AF, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular dilation.

questions.q: Which of the following are recognized complications of long-standing isolated severe mitral stenosis?
e: Severe MS raises left atrial pressure: the dilated atrium fibrillates, the back-pressure produces pulmonary hypertension, and the right ventricle dilates and fails against the raised pulmonary pressure.

questions.q: Mitral valve diseases can lead to:
e: Mitral valve disease raises left atrial pressure and enlarges the atrium: pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and right-sided heart failure all follow from the same upstream pressure load.

questions.q: A patient with mitral stenosis and atrial fibrillation should receive which antithrombotic treatment, and for how long?
questions.sa: Long-term (life-long) anticoagulation with warfarin; it is continued even after balloon mitral valvotomy.
e: Mitral stenosis with AF is valvular AF: lifelong warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist) is required, even after valvotomy. Direct oral anticoagulants are reserved for nonvalvular AF.

questions.q: Balloon (percutaneous) mitral valvotomy is NOT done in:
questions.sa: Significant (severe) mitral regurgitation; valvotomy is reserved for isolated, non-calcified mitral stenosis (also not in calcified valves).
e: Contraindicated in significant MR (and calcified valves).

questions.q: Which of the following clinical findings makes balloon mitral valvotomy probably favorable?
o: A shifted apex to the left 6th space anterior axillary line
An accentuated pulmonary component of the second heart sound
An opening snap after the second heart sound
A pansystolic murmur over the apex
e: Opening snap shows a pliable valve.

questions.q: A 23-year-old female presents to the clinic with shortness of breath on ordinary effort over the last year. BP is 90/60 mmHg, HR is 100/min, and JVP is normal. Examination reveals an apical mid-diastolic rumbling murmur and accentuated P2. The ECG shows P-mitrale and sinus tachycardia. Echocardiography shows tight mitral stenosis with MVA = 0.9 cm². Balloon mitral valvuloplasty would be preferred over surgical mitral valve replacement in this patient EXCEPT in which of the following situations?
e: Significant MR is a contraindication to valvuloplasty.

questions.q: Which of the following is the leading cause of mitral regurgitation in DEVELOPING countries?
e: RHD is the leading cause of MR in developing countries.

questions.q: Which of the following is FALSE regarding the clinical features of mitral regurgitation?
o: Apex shifted outwards and downwards and hyperdynamic in character
Pansystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, increased in the left lateral position
e: Reversed splitting is not a feature of MR.

questions.q: All of the following features are present in the chest X-ray of a patient with mitral regurgitation EXCEPT:
o: Bulge of the waist of the heart, elevation of the left main stem bronchus and double density sign
Oesophagus pushed or curved backward by the enlarged left atrium
e: Coeur en sabot is a Fallot sign.

questions.q: Management of mitral incompetence includes all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Balloon dilatation does not treat MR.

questions.q: What is the best treatment option for a 75-year-old female with symptomatic (NYHA class III) chronic severe rheumatic mitral regurgitation and a heavily calcified mitral valve?
o: Mitral valve replacement with a bioprosthesis
Mitral valve replacement with a mechanical prosthesis
e: A heavily calcified valve cannot be repaired, so replacement is needed; in a 75-year-old a bioprosthesis is preferred because it avoids lifelong anticoagulation, whereas a mechanical valve would commit her to lifelong warfarin.

questions.q: Aortic stenosis can manifest by:
e: The classic symptomatic triad of severe AS: angina (LVH raises oxygen demand while fixed output limits supply), exertional syncope (fixed cardiac output cannot rise with exertional vasodilatation), and heart failure (pressure-overload LV failure).

questions.q: A 73-year-old male presents to the ER because he lost consciousness while working in the garden. He says he has had several episodes of near-syncope on exertion recently. He is not taking any medication. The BP is 110/85 and HR is 80 bpm. Cardiac examination reveals an ejection systolic murmur at the base of the heart with radiation to the carotid arteries. The ECG shows LVH and strain. What is the most probable cause of the patient's syncope?
e: Exertional syncope with an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids and LVH is severe aortic stenosis; in a 73-year-old the cause is age-related sclerocalcific degeneration of the valve, and syncope reflects a fixed cardiac output that cannot meet exertional demand.

questions.q: Signs of severe valvular aortic stenosis include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Weak aortic component of the second heart sound
Early-peaking systolic ejection murmur propagating to the carotids
Paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound
e: AS has a LATE-peaking murmur.

questions.q: Signs of severe valvular aortic stenosis include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Late-peaking systolic ejection murmur propagating to the carotids
Paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound
e: Bisferiens pulse indicates mixed AS/AR, not pure severe AS.

questions.q: Medical treatment of chronic aortic regurgitation is started with which drug class?
questions.sa: Vasodilators (e.g., ACE inhibitors) to reduce peripheral resistance and the regurgitant volume.
e: Vasodilators (ACE inhibitors) are first-line medical therapy.

questions.q: Name two predisposing (etiological) factors for aortic regurgitation other than rheumatic fever.
questions.sa: Marfan's syndrome (dilated ascending aorta) and congenital (bicuspid) aortic valve; also infective endocarditis, syphilitic aortitis, severe hypertension, ankylosing spondylitis, aortic dissection.
e: Marfan and bicuspid valve are common causes.

questions.q: A 36-year-old female patient admitted to the ophthalmology department for lens subluxation is noticed to have a BP of 160/40. You were asked for your opinion regarding management of her hypertension and you noticed that she has a diastolic murmur over the left parasternal region. The following is true regarding this patient EXCEPT:
o: Pistol shots may be auscultated over her femoral artery
The inheritance of this problem is autosomal dominant
She needs long-acting penicillin for life
e: This is Marfan syndrome — autosomal dominant, with dislocated lenses and aortic regurgitation from aortic root disease, giving a wide pulse pressure and peripheral signs such as pistol-shot femorals. Long-acting penicillin prophylaxis is for rheumatic heart disease after rheumatic fever, not for Marfan syndrome, so option D is the exception.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding severe tricuspid regurgitation is correct?
o: The intensity of the tricuspid regurgitation murmur increases during inspiration and leg raising and decreases in the standing position
Cachexia and jaundice could be associated with advanced severe tricuspid regurgitation
Intravenous drug use could be an aetiology for primary tricuspid valve disease
e: The TR murmur increases with inspiration and leg raising (increased venous return to the right heart); long-standing severe TR causes systemic congestion with cardiac cachexia and congestive hepatopathy (jaundice); and intravenous drug use causes tricuspid valve endocarditis, a cause of primary TR.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct?
o: Bioprosthetic valve replacement is the modality of choice in young patients with severe mitral regurgitation
Mechanical valve replacement is the main line of treatment in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation
Disappearance or muffling of the metallic heart sound is a common physiological observation
e: None is correct: young patients receive mechanical valves because bioprostheses degenerate faster in the young; severe TR is usually repaired (e.g. annuloplasty), not replaced; and loss or muffling of the metallic click is not physiological — it suggests prosthetic dysfunction such as thrombosis or obstruction.

questions.q: A 72-year-old woman presented to you complaining of orthopnea. Cardiac auscultation revealed an ejection systolic murmur over the base of the heart propagating to the carotids. What is the life expectancy of this patient if left untreated?
e: Untreated AS with heart failure: survival about 2 years. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: A 72-year-old woman presented to you complaining of syncope following exertion. Cardiac auscultation revealed an ejection systolic murmur over the base of the heart propagating to the carotids. What is the life expectancy of this patient if left untreated?
e: AS with syncope: about 3 years. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: A 72-year-old woman presented to you complaining of exertional chest pain. Cardiac auscultation revealed an ejection systolic murmur over the base of the heart propagating to the carotids. What is the life expectancy of this patient if left untreated?
e: AS with angina: about 5 years. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: Mitral stenosis may be associated with all EXCEPT:
e: MS does not produce ejection systolic murmurs. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: All of the following are contraindications for balloon mitral valvuloplasty in patients with mitral stenosis EXCEPT:
o: Markedly thickened, calcified, immobile leaflets with calcified commissures
f: Severe TR requiring surgery is also a contraindication per guidelines.
e: As keyed in the source: resistant left atrial thrombus, severe mitral regurgitation, and markedly thickened calcified immobile leaflets are contraindications to balloon valvuloplasty; associated severe tricuspid regurgitation alone is not listed. Note: tricuspid disease severe enough to require surgery would favor a surgical approach over a balloon procedure.

questions.q: All of the following are contraindications for balloon mitral valvuloplasty in patients with mitral stenosis EXCEPT:
o: Associated severe aortic regurgitation or aortic stenosis
Markedly thickened, calcified, immobile leaflets with calcified commissures and high Wilkins score
e: Mild MR is not a contraindication. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: Which of the following cardiac structures is responsible for the occurrence of mitral regurgitation?
e: MR can arise from any part of the mitral apparatus: leaflets, a dilated annulus, ruptured chordae, dysfunctional or ruptured papillary muscles, a dilated/dysfunctional left ventricle, and an enlarged left atrium.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an indication for surgery in patients with chronic severe mitral regurgitation?
o: Moderate/severe secondary MR if undergoing CABG
Asymptomatic patients with increased left ventricular diastolic dimensions
e: Increased diastolic dimension alone is not an indication (systolic dimension is). (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: Aortic valve replacement is indicated in the following clinical scenarios:
o: Symptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis
Asymptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis undergoing CABG
Asymptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis and poor LV function
e: AVR in symptomatic AS, AS with CABG, or LV dysfunction. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: Aortic valve replacement is indicated in the following clinical scenarios EXCEPT:
o: Symptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis
Asymptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis undergoing CABG
Asymptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis and poor LV function
Asymptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis
e: Asymptomatic severe AS alone is not an indication. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: To date, what are the indications for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)?
o: Women in the childbearing period with aortic stenosis
High-risk patients for conventional aortic valve surgery
Aortic stenosis in an otherwise healthy young man
e: TAVI is for high-risk surgical candidates. (Keyed per the exam; not covered in the books.)

questions.q: The chief concern in the anesthetic management of a patient with mitral stenosis is to avoid tachycardia because it:
o: Decreases filling time and hence increases the trans-mitral pressure gradient
Reduces the size of the left atrium
e: In mitral stenosis, ventricular filling depends on diastolic time and on atrial contraction: tachycardia shortens diastole, raises left atrial pressure and the trans-mitral gradient, and can precipitate pulmonary edema — so heart rate must be kept controlled.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding patients with mechanical mitral valve prostheses is correct?
o: Should receive warfarin for only three months after surgery
Should receive lone single antiplatelet therapy if the patient is in normal sinus rhythm
Should receive life-long warfarin or direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs)
e: Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist) — not 3 months, not antiplatelet alone, and not a DOAC: direct oral anticoagulants are reserved for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and are contraindicated with mechanical valves.

questions.q: All the following are typical complications of long-standing isolated mitral stenosis except:
e: In isolated MS the LV is normally small/underfilled; LV dilatation is not a typical complication.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding tricuspid valve diseases are correct except:
o: The intensity of tricuspid regurgitation murmur increases during inspiration and leg-raising.
Cachexia and jaundice could be associated with long-standing severe tricuspid regurgitation.
In severe tricuspid regurgitation, jugular venous pressure is usually high with a systolic collapse.
Functional tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is more common than primary TR.
e: In severe TR the JVP shows systolic expansion (large v waves), not collapse.

questions.q: Which is the following statement is correct regarding the clinical findings in a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
o: Ejection systolic murmur which increases with inspiration.
Ejection systolic murmur with early peaking.
Accentuated aortic component of the second heart sound.
Ejection systolic murmur with delayed peaking.
e: Severe AS has a late (delayed) peaking ejection systolic murmur.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes mechanical mitral valve replacement. Six months later, she asks her cardiologist whether she can switch from warfarin to rivaroxaban for convenience. What is the best response?
o: Switching is safe because DOACs have been shown to be non-inferior to warfarin for mechanical valves.
She can switch to rivaroxaban only if she is in normal sinus rhythm.
Switching is contraindicated; lifelong warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist) is the only approved anticoagulation strategy for mechanical heart valves.
She can switch to aspirin alone since more than three months have passed since surgery.
e: Mechanical valves require lifelong warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated.

questions.q: The following signs should be checked in patients with infective endocarditis EXCEPT:
e: Fever, new murmur, splenomegaly (~20% of cases) and clubbing (a late sign) are all part of the IE picture — so none is the exception.

questions.q: Which of the following is a major Duke's criterion?
o: A single positive blood culture for typical organism
e: A single positive culture for a typical organism is only a minor criterion — major requires 2 separate positive cultures; echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation) is a major criterion.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male patient presenting with persistent fever for 2 weeks; he is a known IV drug abuser, his virology was positive for HCV but not for HBV or HIV. What should you suspect?
e: IV drug use predisposes to right-sided (tricuspid) S. aureus endocarditis; the exam keys the methicillin-resistant form.

questions.q: Prophylaxis against endocarditis for predisposed patients is indicated in which condition?
e: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures in high-risk patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the ER with 3 hours of chest pain at rest. He recently had an upper respiratory tract infection. HR 80/min, BP 120/80, RR 20. Physical examination, laboratory tests and chest X-ray are normal. His ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
f: Same vignette as Q341 (pericarditis) but a different ECG image; keyed as myocarditis.
e: Chest pain at rest in a young man shortly after a viral upper respiratory infection, with normal examination, laboratory tests and chest X-ray, points to acute myocarditis — post-viral myocardial inflammation that mimics acute ischemia in a patient without coronary risk factors.

questions.q: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by:
o: Usually inherited as an autosomal dominant disease
Being a common cause of sudden death in young subjects under age 35 years
e: All three hold: HCM is usually autosomal dominant, shows marked (typically septal) hypertrophy, and is a common cause of sudden death in young subjects under 35 — the book's cardiomyopathy table likewise flags syncope and sudden-death risk in HCM.

questions.q: A 22-year-old athletic person reports an episode of syncope after vigorous field play. Which cardiac disease should you rule out in this patient?
e: Exertional syncope in a young athlete mandates ruling out HCM: dynamic outflow obstruction and ventricular arrhythmias during exertion can cause syncope and sudden death — the book's cardiomyopathy table lists syncope + sudden-death risk for HCM.

questions.q: A patient came complaining of retrosternal chest pain of few days duration; the pain doesn't change with exertion but decreases on sitting forward. What is the most probable diagnosis?
e: Pain relieved by sitting forward: pericarditis.

questions.q: Acute pericarditis is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
o: Chest pain that becomes worse when lying down and improves on sitting up and leaning forward
ECG shows diffuse concave-upward ST segment elevation
ECG shows convex-upward ST segment elevation in the anterior chest leads with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads
ECG shows diffuse PR segment depression
e: Convex ST elevation with reciprocal depression = STEMI, not pericarditis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency room with 3 hours of chest pain at rest. Recently, he had an upper respiratory tract infection. His heart rate is 80/min, blood pressure 120/80, and respiratory rate 20/min. Physical examination is normal. Laboratory tests and chest X-ray are normal. His ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Diffuse ST elevation and PR depression after viral illness: pericarditis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency room with 3 hours of chest pain at rest that improves by leaning forward. Recently, he had an upper respiratory tract infection. His heart rate is 80/min, blood pressure 120/80, and respiratory rate 20/min. Physical examination is normal. Laboratory tests and chest X-ray are normal. His ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Diffuse concave ST elevation, pain relieved leaning forward: pericarditis.

questions.q: Which of the following finding(s) is/are observed in a patient with cardiac tamponade?
e: Beck triad: hypotension, raised JVP, distant heart sounds.

questions.q: Features of cardiac tamponade include:
e: All are features of tamponade.

questions.q: A 49-year-old female with a history of smoking for 20 years presents to the cardiology clinic with progressive shortness of breath after a flu-like illness. Her BP is 80/60 and ECG shows electrical alternans. Two-D echo is shown. Beck's triad of pericardial tamponade includes the following EXCEPT:
e: Tachycardia is not part of Beck triad.

questions.q: Signs of pericardial tamponade include all the following EXCEPT:
e: JVP is raised in tamponade.

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE regarding cardiac tamponade?
o: Pericardiocentesis is needed only after full work-up for the etiology
Immediate inotropic agents are essential for management
Jugular venous pressure is usually high
Bradycardia is a frequent clinical finding
e: JVP high in tamponade.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding cardiac tamponade are correct EXCEPT:
o: Sinus bradycardia is an early sign
Coronary perforation during PCI could cause a cardiac tamponade
e: Tachycardia, not bradycardia, is an early sign.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding cardiac tamponade are correct EXCEPT:
o: Sinus tachycardia is an early sign
Diuretics are the main line of therapy
e: Pericardiocentesis, not diuretics, is treatment.

questions.q: The following regarding cardiac tamponade is correct EXCEPT:
o: Use of positive inotropics in management
e: Tamponade is mechanical compression of diastolic filling — only removing fluid (pericardiocentesis) relieves it; inotropes do not treat the cause.

questions.q: All of the following regarding cardiac tamponade is correct EXCEPT:
e: Lungs are clear in tamponade.

questions.q: Increased JVP with hypotension occurs in:
e: RV MI and tamponade both give raised JVP and hypotension.

questions.q: In a patient with low blood pressure and raised jugular venous pressure, which of the following would make a diagnosis of pericardial tamponade LESS likely?
o: A large heart shadow on the chest X-ray
Failure to show a pericardial effusion by echocardiography
e: No effusion on echo makes tamponade unlikely.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female patient known to have lupus presented to the ER with disturbed conscious level; her BP is inaudible, her heart sounds are distant and her neck veins are elevated. She was started on inotropes but with no response. Her chest X-ray is shown. What is the diagnosis?
e: Lupus, shock, distant sounds, raised JVP, flask heart: tamponade.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female patient known to have lupus presented to the ER with disturbed conscious level; her BP is inaudible, her heart sounds are distant and her neck veins are elevated. She was started on inotropes but with no response. Her chest X-ray is shown (flask-shaped cardiac silhouette). The main line of treatment of this condition is:
e: Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis is the life-saving treatment of tamponade; inotropes and antibiotics do not relieve the mechanical compression.

questions.q: Is bradycardia a feature of constrictive pericarditis?
questions.sa: No. The fixed, limited stroke volume is compensated by TACHYCARDIA (and AF in about one third); the other features are a small-volume pulse, pulsus paradoxus, raised JVP with Kussmaul's sign and prominent x and y descents, a pericardial knock and hepatomegaly/ascites.
e: Constrictive pericarditis shows tachycardia, not bradycardia.

questions.q: A 63-year-old man presents to the emergency room complaining of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back of 2 hours duration. The examination revealed a pulse of 120/min with a pulse volume weaker on the right arm than the left. The BP was measured 110/80 on the right arm and 180/100 on the left arm. The cardiac examination revealed an early diastolic murmur over the aortic area. The chest examination was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Tearing pain radiating to the back with unequal arm pulses/BP and a new early diastolic (AR) murmur = Stanford type A (proximal/ascending) dissection: the tear involves the ascending aorta and arch vessels, and AR follows when the dissection disrupts the aortic valve support.

questions.q: A patient with severe tearing retrosternal pain and unequal blood pressure in both upper limbs (180/110 in the left, 110/80 in the right):
e: Tearing retrosternal pain with unequal UPPER-limb pressures implicates the arch vessels, i.e. a proximal (Stanford type A) dissection; type B affects only the descending aorta.

questions.q: Severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back with unequal pulses increases the possibility of which of the following conditions?
e: Tearing pain radiating to the back with unequal pulses is the classic presentation of aortic dissection: an intimal tear lets blood split the media into true and false lumens.

questions.q: A 54-year-old man presents to the ER 3 hours after the onset of severe tearing substernal chest pain. Examination reveals a pale male who is anxious and diaphoretic. The BP was 95/70 in the right arm and 75/50 mmHg in the left arm. Bedside echo shows moderate pericardial effusion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Tearing substernal pain with unequal arm BPs = aortic dissection (severe retrosternal pain with unequal upper-limb pulses); the pericardial effusion reflects blood reaching the pericardial sac as the dissection extends proximally.

questions.q: A 44-year-old man presents to the ER 3 hours after the onset of severe tearing substernal chest pain. He is pale, anxious and diaphoretic. BP is 140/70 in the right arm and 75/50 mmHg in the left arm. Cardiac examination reveals mild aortic regurgitation. The ECG shows LVH and strain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Tearing pain + unequal arm BPs + aortic regurgitation = Stanford type A dissection: the AR murmur signals ascending-aorta involvement, i.e. the proximal type.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female presents to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back. She is 180 cm tall with long extremities. Her joints show significant hyperextensibility. BP is 170/70 on the right arm and 120/60 on the left arm. HR is 100/min regular. Which of the following additional findings is also likely in this patient?
o: Fourth heart sound over the apex
Early diastolic murmur over the aortic area
Opening snap over the left parasternal area
Wide fixed splitting of the second heart sound
e: Tall stature, long extremities and hyperextensible joints = Marfan syndrome, a cause of aortic dissection; the expected added finding is the early diastolic murmur of acute aortic regurgitation from ascending-aorta involvement.

questions.q: Marfan's syndrome may be associated with all the following EXCEPT:
e: Marfan syndrome causes mitral valve prolapse, aortic regurgitation and acute aortic dissection (medial necrosis / aneurysmal disease of the aorta) — but not aortic stenosis.

questions.q: A 44-year-old man presents to the ER 3 hours after the onset of severe tearing substernal chest pain. He is pale, anxious and diaphoretic. The BP is 140/70 in the right arm and 75/50 mmHg in the left arm. Cardiac examination reveals mild aortic regurgitation. The ECG shows LVH and strain. Which of the following is the recommended diagnostic tool?
e: CT angiography (MSCT) shows the intimal flap separating the true and false lumens. The book's diagnostic list is: clinical suspicion (hypertensive patient, chest pain, unequal pulse), plain CXR (widened mediastinum), TEE, CT angiography and MRA.

questions.q: The main diagnostic modality in aortic dissection is:
e: CT aortography is the main imaging modality: it demonstrates the intimal flap and the true/false lumens. CXR only shows a widened mediastinum; TEE and MRA are alternatives.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding aortic dissection are correct EXCEPT:
o: Stanford type A aortic dissection may cause an acute aortic regurgitation.
Hypertension is a risk factor for acute aortic dissection.
Stanford type A acute aortic dissection is usually managed medically.
CT aortography is the main imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis.
e: Type A (ascending) dissection requires emergency surgery — surgery is virtually always indicated for the ascending aorta because of life-threatening complications. Medical therapy (beta-blockers + BP reduction to ~100–120 systolic) is the bridge, not the definitive treatment. Hypertension is a risk factor and CT aortography is the main imaging modality.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding pulmonary hypertension (PH) are correct EXCEPT:
o: Left heart disease is a rare cause of PH
Eisenmenger syndrome is associated with pulmonary hypertension
Chest disease is one of the etiologies of pulmonary hypertension
PH usually accentuates the pulmonary component of the second heart sound
e: Left heart disease is the commonest cause of PH.

questions.q: All of the following statements regarding pulmonary hypertension (PH) are correct EXCEPT:
o: Mitral valve disease could cause a post-capillary PH
Eisenmenger syndrome entails a pulmonary hypertension pathophysiology
