Chest diseases are among the causes of pulmonary hypertension
The pulmonary component of the second heart sound is muffled in PH
e: P2 is accentuated (loud) in PH.

questions.q: Which of the following is correct regarding pulmonary hypertension?
o: Muffling of the pulmonary component of S2
Accentuation of the pulmonary component of S2
Pulmonary stenosis is one of the most common etiologies
e: Accentuated P2.

questions.q: Which statement is true regarding severe pulmonary hypertension?
o: Splitting of the first heart sound
Muffled pulmonary component of the second heart sound
Accentuated pulmonary component of the second heart sound
Cardiac apex is localized and shifted to the left 6th anterior axillary line
e: Accentuated P2.

questions.q: Clinical sign(s) of severe pulmonary hypertension:
o: Muffled pulmonary component of the second heart sound
Cardiac apex is localized and shifted to the left 6th anterior axillary line
e: Severe PH: congested pulsating neck veins.

questions.q: All of the following are suggestive of pulmonary hypertension EXCEPT:
o: Palpable pulsation in the pulmonary area
e: Reversed splitting is not a PH sign.

questions.q: A patient with pulmonary embolism can present with:
e: PE presents with acute dyspnoea, tachypnoea, pleuritic chest pain and sometimes haemoptysis; massive emboli cause cardiovascular collapse — syncope, hypotension, sudden death.

questions.q: A patient with pulmonary embolism can present with:
e: Sinus tachycardia is common in PE and syncope occurs with massive PE; the ECG may show RV strain with S in lead I, Q in lead III and T in lead III (S1Q3T3) in ~20% of cases, new RBBB or new AF.

questions.q: A 63-year-old man presents to the ER complaining of shortness of breath at rest and one attack of hemoptysis 2 hours before presentation. He gives a history of knee surgery 1 week before presentation. The pulse was 130/min with a pulse volume equal on both arms and normal peripheral pulsations. The BP was 90/60 equal on both arms. Blood gases revealed low PO2 and low PCO2. Cardiac examination revealed a loud P2 with a third heart sound over the tricuspid area. Chest examination revealed normal vesicular breathing with bilateral rhonchi. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Recent surgery (immobilisation — Virchow's triad) + dyspnoea, haemoptysis, hypoxia with hypocapnia from reflex hyperventilation, and a loud P2 with RV strain = pulmonary embolism. Equal arm pulses/BP argue against dissection.

questions.q: A 65-year-old patient presents with shortness of breath at rest. All the following features are highly suspicious of pulmonary embolism EXCEPT:
e: Bilateral basal rales suggest LV failure, not PE.

questions.q: All the following features are highly suspicious of pulmonary embolism EXCEPT:
o: Blood gases showing low PO2 and low PCO2
e: Sinus tachycardia (not bradycardia) is common in PE.

questions.q: A 78-year-old female with history of hip replacement 2 weeks ago. Her right lower limb is swollen for 3 days. She presents to the ER with acute shortness of breath. Pulmonary embolism is confirmed by MSCT pulmonary angiography. The following ECG changes are common EXCEPT:
e: Sinus tachycardia, AF and S1Q3T3 occur; bradycardia is not typical.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents to the ER; he has been immobile for the past 6 weeks following an orthopedic operation for a left femur fracture. He developed sudden shortness of breath associated with chest pain. Vitals: BP 100/62 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, temperature 36.7 C, RR 28/min, SpO2 88% (room air). There are no clinical signs of a DVT. What is the most appropriate investigation to reach a definite diagnosis for this case scenario?
e: Spiral CT (CT pulmonary angiography) is the imaging modality of choice for PE and detects small emboli accurately. Catheter pulmonary angiography is the gold standard but invasive; CXR is often normal and troponin does not diagnose PE.

questions.q: A 78-year-old female patient with a history of hip replacement 2 weeks ago, who had right lower limb swelling for 3 days, presented to the ER with acute shortness of breath, tachycardia and pleuritic chest pain. She is vitally stable; her ECG was normal apart from sinus tachycardia. The most appropriate next step is:
e: Suspected PE in a stable patient: start anticoagulation immediately (unfractionated heparin or LMWH) and arrange prompt CT pulmonary angiography for definitive diagnosis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old female on oral contraceptive pills presented complaining of shortness of breath and pleuritic pain. She reports a history of right lower limb swelling of one week duration. On examination she has a normal respiratory rate with oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Heart rate was 105 beats per minute and blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg. Which of the following is the best next step?
o: Thrombolytic therapy should be started immediately
Start low molecular weight heparin and order CT pulmonary angiography
e: Haemodynamically stable suspected PE (OCP + leg swelling + pleuritic pain): start LMWH immediately and order CT pulmonary angiography. Thrombolysis is reserved for PE with haemodynamic instability — this patient is stable — and coronary angiography is not indicated.

questions.q: What is the treatment of choice in a patient with pulmonary embolism presenting with severe shortness of breath and who is in shock?
e: PE with shock = massive (haemodynamically unstable) PE: thrombolytics are indicated — they lyse the clot by activating fibrinolysis. Anticoagulants alone do not dissolve an obstructing embolus fast enough in shock.
